title: Lecture 2 slides (Wednesday, 2026-11-04)
text:
The slides the instructor taught from, as published on the course website: their text, the R code, and the output each piece of code printed. Plots are not included; the code before each [Plot] marker draws it. Each heading links to its section on the website.




library(tidyverse)



The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.



Here’s the tidy Billboard data from Lecture 1’s Tidy data section.
billboard_tidy <- read_csv("data/billboard.csv") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |>
  arrange(artist, track, week) |>
  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)
Rows: 317 Columns: 81
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr   (2): artist, track
dbl  (66): year, wk1, wk2, wk3, wk4, wk5, wk6, wk7, wk8, wk9, wk10, wk11, wk...
lgl  (11): wk66, wk67, wk68, wk69, wk70, wk71, wk72, wk73, wk74, wk75, wk76
date  (1): date.entered
time  (1): time

  distinct(artist, track, year, time) |>
  mutate(id = row_number(), .before = 1)

The opposite problem is one kind of observation split across many files, such as one file per year or one per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them with bind_rows() or give read_csv() all the file names at once.



Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule, with one table per kind of observational unit, linked by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake but realistic patient records stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients in CSV, HL7 FHIR, and C-CDA formats.



In practice, health data is usually stored and shared using data standards, not as a folder of CSV files.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, which sends a patient, an encounter, or an observation as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on many hospitals’ databases

All of these follow the third rule, with one table (or resource) per kind of observational unit, linked by IDs.




billboard.csv: the tidy data paper’s Billboard example, via chendaniely/pandas_for_everyone and hadley/tidy-data
Wickham, H. (2014). Tidy Data. Journal of Statistical Software, 59(10). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10 (PDF: https://vita.had.co.nz/papers/tidy-data.pdf)
Synthea synthetic patient records: https://synthetichealth.github.io/synthea/
Standards: HL7, FHIR, OHDSI and its OMOP Common Data Model.







library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)



On Monday we fit price ~ sqft on the Sacramento house sales. Let’s add type, a categorical variable, so we can see how to read both kinds of variables.
Sacramento |>
  count(type)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  type             n
  <fct>        <int>
1 Condo           53
2 Multi_Family    13
3 Residential    866




A regression needs numbers, so R turns a categorical variable (a factor) into dummy variables, also called indicator variables
Each dummy variable is a 0/1 column for one level, and there’s one for every level except the first
The level without a column is the reference level, and every other level gets compared with it





Statistics calls this dummy variable encoding
Computer science and machine learning call it one-hot encoding
Both turn each level of a categorical variable into a 0/1 column
One-hot encoding usually keeps a column for every level, while a regression with an intercept drops one, the reference level (R does this for us)




type has 3 levels, so it becomes 2 dummy variables, with Condo as the reference:



type
typeMulti_Family
typeResidential




Condo
0
0


Multi_Family
1
0


Residential
0
1






house_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento)

house_tidy <- tidy(house_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
house_tidy
# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term             estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         6885.  12169.       0.566 5.72e-  1  -16996.    30766.
2 sqft                 139.      3.88    35.7   1.64e-176     131.      146.
3 typeMulti_Family  -66224.  26222.      -2.53  1.17e-  2 -117686.   -14762.
4 typeResidential     8253.  12151.       0.679 4.97e-  1  -15594.    32100.

One row for sqft
One row for each dummy variable, and no row for Condo, the reference level





For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect [outcome] to increase (or decrease) by [estimate] [units], all else remaining the same.

For sqft:

For every 1 square foot increase in size, we expect the sale price to increase by $139, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $131 to $146).


“All else remaining the same” means the other variables in the model, so here, a house of the same type





We expect [outcome] for [level] to be [estimate] [units] higher (or lower) than for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For typeMulti_Family:

We expect multi-family homes to sell for $66,224 less than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $14,762 to $117,686 less).


Here “all else” is the size: a multi-family home and a condo with the same square footage
The comparison is always with the reference level, Condo




For typeResidential:

We expect residential homes to sell for $8,253 more than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: -$15,594 to $32,100).


The interval includes 0, so the data don’t show a clear difference between residential homes and condos of the same size
We still report the estimate and its interval, and say that it’s unclear





The intercept is the expected outcome when every continuous variable is 0 and every categorical variable is at its reference level
Here that’s a condo with 0 square feet, which doesn’t exist, so we don’t interpret it




Base R’s lm() fits the same model with less code:
lm(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento) |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE)
# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term             estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         6885.  12169.       0.566 5.72e-  1  -16996.    30766.
2 sqft                 139.      3.88    35.7   1.64e-176     131.      146.
3 typeMulti_Family  -66224.  26222.      -2.53  1.17e-  2 -117686.   -14762.
4 typeResidential     8253.  12151.       0.679 4.97e-  1  -15594.    32100.

The same estimates and intervals as linear_reg()
We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps





Sacramento: from modeldata, loaded with tidymodels
Interpreting coefficients follows chapter 8 of Data Science: A First Introduction and the analysis chapter of Data Science for the Biomedical Sciences







library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)



licorice_gargle (from medicaldata) is a trial of 235 adults having thoracic surgery with a large breathing tube. Before the tube went in, they were randomized to gargle licorice or sugar water. Our outcome is any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.



sore <- licorice_gargle |>
  mutate(
    sore_throat = factor(pacu30min_throatPain > 0,
                         levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("no", "yes")),
    treatment = factor(treat, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("sugar", "licorice")),
    smoking = factor(preOp_smoking, levels = c(3, 2, 1),
                     labels = c("never", "past",
                                "current"))
  ) |>
  select(sore_throat, treatment,
         bmi = preOp_calcBMI, smoking) |>
  drop_na()




logistic_reg() models the odds of the outcome’s second level
sore_throat has the levels no, then yes, so every result is about the odds of a sore throat
The predictors are a mix of both kinds:

treatment: 2 levels, so 1 dummy variable (reference sugar)
bmi: continuous, in kg/m²
smoking: 3 levels, so 2 dummy variables (reference never)


count(sore, sore_throat)
  sore_throat   n
1          no 169
2         yes  64



sore_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
      data = sore)

tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         0.0240    0.979     0.0245 0.980      -1.91     1.95  
2 treatmentlicorice  -0.956     0.316    -3.02   0.00252    -1.59    -0.346 
3 bmi                -0.0517    0.0385   -1.34   0.179      -0.129    0.0229
4 smokingpast         1.48      0.428     3.45   0.000551    0.664    2.35  
5 smokingcurrent      0.635     0.410     1.55   0.121      -0.152    1.46  

These estimates are on the log-odds scale, \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)\), which is hard to read




sore_or <- sore_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
sore_or
# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 

exponentiate = TRUE turns each estimate and its interval into an odds ratio (std.error, statistic, and p.value stay on the log-odds scale)
An odds ratio of 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower odds, and above 1 means higher odds





For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio], all else remaining the same.

For bmi:

For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI, we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by 0.95, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.88 to 1.02).


Multiplied by 0.95 is the same as 5% lower odds
The interval includes 1, so the data don’t show a clear effect of BMI





We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level] to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For treatmentlicorice:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice to be 0.38 times the odds for patients who gargled sugar water, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.71).


That’s 62% lower odds, and the interval doesn’t include 1




Each dummy variable compares one level with the reference, never. For smokingpast:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for past smokers to be 4.38 times the odds for people who never smoked, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 1.94 to 10.48).


smokingcurrent compares current smokers with people who never smoked, not with past smokers
Its interval (0.86 to 4.33) includes 1, so that comparison isn’t clear





An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities
Say “0.38 times the odds”, not “0.38 times as likely” or “62% less likely”
The two are close only when the outcome is rare, and here 27% of patients had a sore throat




Base R’s glm() fits the same model with less code:
glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
    family = binomial, data = sore) |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 

family = binomial is what makes glm() a logistic regression
The same odds ratios and intervals as logistic_reg()
We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps





licorice_gargle from medicaldata, contributed by Amy Nowacki (TSHS Resources Portal)
Odds ratios with tidymodels follow the analysis and tidymodels chapters of Data Science for the Biomedical Sciences

For sqft:

For every 1 square foot increase in size, we expect the sale price to increase by $139, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $131 to $146).


“All else remaining the same” means the other variables in the model, so here, a house of the same type

We still report the estimate and its interval, and say that it’s unclear

Here that’s a condo with 0 square feet, which doesn’t exist, so we don’t interpret it

title: Lecture 2 slides (Wednesday, 2026-11-04)
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)



licorice_gargle (from medicaldata) is a trial of 235 adults having thoracic surgery with a large breathing tube. Before the tube went in, they were randomized to gargle licorice or sugar water. Our outcome is any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.



sore <- licorice_gargle |>
  mutate(
    sore_throat = factor(pacu30min_throatPain > 0,
                         levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("no", "yes")),
    treatment = factor(treat, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("sugar", "licorice")),
    smoking = factor(preOp_smoking, levels = c(3, 2, 1),
                     labels = c("never", "past",
                                "current"))
  ) |>
  select(sore_throat, treatment,
         bmi = preOp_calcBMI, smoking) |>
  drop_na()




logistic_reg() models the odds of the outcome’s second level
sore_throat has the levels no, then yes, so every result is about the odds of a sore throat
The predictors are a mix of both kinds:

treatment: 2 levels, so 1 dummy variable (reference sugar)
bmi: continuous, in kg/m²
smoking: 3 levels, so 2 dummy variables (reference never)


count(sore, sore_throat)
  sore_throat   n
1          no 169
2         yes  64



sore_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
      data = sore)

tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         0.0240    0.979     0.0245 0.980      -1.91     1.95  
2 treatmentlicorice  -0.956     0.316    -3.02   0.00252    -1.59    -0.346 
3 bmi                -0.0517    0.0385   -1.34   0.179      -0.129    0.0229
4 smokingpast         1.48      0.428     3.45   0.000551    0.664    2.35  
5 smokingcurrent      0.635     0.410     1.55   0.121      -0.152    1.46  

These estimates are on the log-odds scale, \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)\), which is hard to read




sore_or <- sore_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
sore_or
# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 

exponentiate = TRUE turns each estimate and its interval into an odds ratio (std.error, statistic, and p.value stay on the log-odds scale)
An odds ratio of 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower odds, and above 1 means higher odds





For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio], all else remaining the same.

For bmi:

For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI, we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by 0.95, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.88 to 1.02).


Multiplied by 0.95 is the same as 5% lower odds
The interval includes 1, so the data don’t show a clear effect of BMI





We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level] to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For treatmentlicorice:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice to be 0.38 times the odds for patients who gargled sugar water, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.71).


That’s 62% lower odds, and the interval doesn’t include 1




Each dummy variable compares one level with the reference, never. For smokingpast:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for past smokers to be 4.38 times the odds for people who never smoked, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 1.94 to 10.48).


smokingcurrent compares current smokers with people who never smoked, not with past smokers
Its interval (0.86 to 4.33) includes 1, so that comparison isn’t clear





An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities
Say “0.38 times the odds”, not “0.38 times as likely” or “62% less likely”
The two are close only when the outcome is rare, and here 27% of patients had a sore throat




Base R’s glm() fits the same model with less code:
glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
    family = binomial, data = sore) |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Summary
Daniel Chen covered how to access course materials and complete homework through GitHub, Codespaces, or a local setup using RStudio or Positron. He demonstrated Quarto workflows and troubleshooting, explained how to preserve work in Codespaces, and discussed the course’s AI-generated notes and summaries.
The lectures also covered tidy data and database design, synthetic and standardized healthcare data, and linear and logistic regression. Students learned to prepare and inspect data, fit models, interpret coefficients, and distinguish predictions from coefficient interpretations. Demonstrations with AI coding agents emphasized incremental prompting, careful review of code and results, and protecting sensitive data.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Knowledge Points

1. Accessing course materials and setting up a workspace

Course repository and Codespaces

Students need a GitHub account to access the course repository. On its GitHub page, select Code, open the Codespaces tab, and choose the option to create or open a Codespace, typically on the main branch. Initial setup may take around ten minutes.
Codespaces may sleep or shut down after inactivity. Returning to the same Codespace preserves its work; restarting it may be faster after the first setup.
If GitHub reports that the maximum number of Codespaces has been reached, visit github.com/codespaces, delete unused instances, and try again. Check the source and name of each instance before deleting anything. A stopped instance can be restarted; do not delete the one containing work you want to keep.
A Codespace can be opened from a fork, but forking is not required for lectures or homework.

Accessing materials without Git or Codespaces

The rendered course site contains lecture materials, with slides and related content in the left-hand navigation. The link to the GitHub repository is near the top-right of the site.
Students can select Download ZIP on GitHub to get the homework files and work locally. The instructor noted that Git is not required. Students can also copy and paste assignment materials as needed.
Repository files, including datasets and slides, are included in the downloaded folder, and the homework file is at the top level.
Local work requires R and an IDE such as RStudio or Positron. Quarto may need to be installed separately. Codespaces is already configured with the required tools and packages.

R, Quarto, and package setup

Local setup instructions explain how to install Quarto and the packages used in the course. Tidyverse should already have been installed for an earlier week; the course introduces tidymodels and healthcare datasets from the medicaldata package.
Students can run the provided package-installation commands in the RStudio console. Reinstalling or updating tidyverse is fine; those who already have it may skip that step.
Quarto is used to create HTML and PDF homework outputs. It can be installed from the Quarto website for the relevant operating system. The instructor recommends installing it separately for a smoother local experience.

Positron, RStudio, and VS Code

Positron is an optional IDE from the people behind RStudio. It is built on VS Code and incorporates familiar RStudio-style data science features, including a variable viewer, console, terminal, and plot viewer. It supports R and Python.
Codespaces is based on VS Code, so its interface differs from local RStudio or Positron. For example, Codespaces does not show the same variable viewer; students can inspect variables by printing them in a code chunk.
In VS Code, install the Quarto extension through the Extensions panel if it is not already present. It is already installed in the course Codespaces and included in Positron. In RStudio, use Render when Quarto is installed.




2. Quarto documents, rendering, and preserving work

Previewing and rendering

Positron has a Preview button. In Codespaces, use the Command Palette if a Preview option is not visible. Open it with Control+Shift+P, Command+Shift+P, or Apple+Shift+P, or use the interface button; type > to enter command-finding mode.
Rendering a Quarto document runs its code, captures the output, and can produce HTML and PDF files. The intended homework deliverables include the Quarto source file and its rendered HTML and PDF versions. Grading alternatives may be available if rendering fails, but completing the setup is also a learning objective.
Quarto combines code, output, and explanatory prose in one reproducible document. Code can be run from top to bottom, with explanations alongside it. It supports reports, websites, and presentations, and works with multiple programming languages.
Quarto is the successor to R Markdown; R Markdown remains supported but is not expected to receive new features. Quarto’s code-cell syntax resembles R Markdown’s, while Quarto bundles capabilities that otherwise may require separate R Markdown packages.
To work in traditional R Markdown, students can copy the .qmd contents into an .rmd file and remove Quarto-specific formatting lines before rendering.

Saving Codespaces work

Work is saved in the specific Codespace instance, not automatically back to Git, even if the student has forked the repository.
Closing the browser tab or allowing the Codespace to time out does not delete the work. Returning to the same named instance preserves it. Deleting the Codespace permanently deletes its work.
The simplest recommended way to preserve homework is to copy the QMD contents and save them in a local file. Students familiar with Git can use the VS Code Git interface to add, commit, and push changes to their fork.
Forking the course repository creates a personal copy that remains available if the instructor’s repository is deleted. If the instructor updates the original repository, Sync from Upstream can bring changes into the fork. Syncing takes additional steps; the instructor said they would try to avoid changing homework files.




3. AI-generated course notes and coding assistants

Course notes and model comparisons

The course site has an AI class notes section containing lecture transcripts and AI-generated summaries. The current lecture’s notes were expected to be available by the end of November 4, 2026.
Students can use headings and summaries to check their understanding, then consult the corresponding transcript or detailed notes as needed.
The instructor records lectures and uses transcripts to generate summaries with an Anthropic model. Course materials also include outputs from local models, allowing students to compare different models’ summaries of the same material. The instructor’s notes may be particularly detailed because the generation prompt requests substantial detail; the prompt is included with the materials.

Using coding agents effectively

Coding agents can inspect project files, write and run code, and suggest file edits. Their capabilities differ from those of a web-based chatbot, and their access to local files creates additional risks.
For learning, ask an agent to handle one small step or code chunk at a time—roughly five lines—rather than generating a large script all at once. Smaller changes are easier to review and understand.
Provide specific prompts with relevant context, technical terms, and directions. Students can name a course function they want the agent to use, ask why it chose another method, or ask it to explain unfamiliar code.
Models and settings differ in speed, cost, and level of explanation. CodeSpaces may use a smaller, less deliberative model, while a higher-thinking model may take longer and provide more detail. Review generated code particularly carefully, regardless of the model.

Reviewing agent output and visualizations

An agent can make plausible but incorrect edits. In one demonstration, it placed code for the next problem where the requested data-cleaning code belonged. Human approval prompts provide a safeguard, but students must still check the changes.
Run generated code, inspect intermediate results, and confirm that they make sense. Fewer syntax errors do not prove that the code performed the right operation.
Model-generated descriptions of figures can also be wrong. In a demonstration using mtcars, a figure had been altered to show a positive relationship between horsepower and miles per gallon, but the model described the usual negative relationship instead. Check interpretations against the actual data and figure.
A useful workflow is to draft a rough figure caption or description yourself, then ask the model to improve or rephrase it.

Privacy and security

Agents may write and run code that prints data frames or other file contents for inspection. That output can be transmitted to third-party model providers, potentially exposing sensitive information such as patient names or medical record numbers.
An agent with file access might encounter credentials or other sensitive files and could potentially take damaging actions, such as exposing information or deleting data. Review requests before approving changes.
Do not use personal AI subscriptions or unsanctioned agents with clinical or other sensitive data. Healthcare or enterprise use requires organization-approved deployments, secure hosting, and established data-sharing agreements.




4. Tidy data, database structure, and healthcare datasets

Tidy data and observational units

Tidy-data principles include organizing each type of observational unit as a table; a commonly cited formulation also says each cell should contain one bit of information.
Identifying observational units helps with cleaning and storage. Analysis-ready data may already be combined, but analysts building datasets or saving data to databases may need to decide what belongs in separate tables and how those tables relate.

Analysis-ready data versus storage-efficient tables

In the Billboard example, pivot_longer() reshapes week columns so each row represents a song’s ranking for a particular week.
A combined tidy table can repeat details such as artist, track, year, and time many times for the same song. This is useful for analysis and modeling, but inefficient for storage and prone to inconsistent corrections.
A storage-oriented design can put each song’s details in a song table with a unique song ID, and store its weekly date and rank in a separate rankings table. The original analysis table can be reconstructed by joining the tables on the ID.
Assigning a unique ID is similar to assigning a medical record number (MRN) to a patient. In hospital data, patient demographics can be kept in a patients table and events in an encounters table; the MRN links them. A demographic correction then needs to be made in one place.
Joining patient and encounter records can support analyses such as estimating the average age of patients receiving an X-ray. MRNs are highly private because they can connect a record to an individual’s demographics and events.

Synthetic and standardized healthcare data

Synthea provides synthetic hospital-like datasets in CSV and healthcare-related formats such as HL7, FHIR, CDA, and CCDA. Dataset sizes range from small examples to hundreds of thousands or even a million patients. It is available for practice, but is not required for the homework.
The OHDSI community’s OMOP Common Data Model standardizes healthcare data structures. When institutions use the same model, analysts can share code for another hospital to run on its own data instead of transferring protected patient records.
OMOP can support standardized coding and mappings across systems, including mappings between ICD-10 and codes used in other countries. Multi-site analysis depends on participating institutions structuring their data according to the shared model.
Healthcare analyses may require joining multiple tables. For example, studying 30-day readmissions after a heart attack may require encounters to identify visits, patient data for demographics, and an appropriate heart-attack code. Analysts should not assume they will receive a preassembled dataset.




5. Data tidying and date handling

Ebola dataset tidying

The homework uses data-tidying operations such as pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), and mutate().
In the Ebola dataset, cells contain combined information that must be separated. Repeated column patterns suggest using pivot_longer() on relevant columns while excluding date and day.
Inspect intermediate results: the first reshape may leave case and death information combined or otherwise unsuitable for analysis, requiring a pivot_wider() step to separate them.
The assignment asks students to produce a frequency table for each country showing the first and last report and the corresponding cases and deaths, and to create and describe a figure from a selected column.

Date parsing

The demonstrated source date column was character text in month-day-year format. An MDY parsing function converts it into a date object.
A date object supports operations such as subtracting one date from another. It may display in year-month-day order because that is the ISO 8601 standard, even if the input was month-day-year.
Use the corresponding YMD parser for year-month-day input. The display format alone does not indicate that parsing was incorrect.




6. Regression: choosing and preparing a model

Linear and logistic regression as baselines

Linear and logistic regression are useful first models: they are relatively simple, run quickly, and are generally easier to interpret than more complex approaches. “Best” is comparative, so these models can provide baselines.
Interpretability can matter in healthcare and finance, where people may need to explain treatment, policy, or financial decisions. These models are not universally superior, and the lectures focus on fitting and interpreting models rather than comprehensively evaluating them.
Linear regression is appropriate for a continuous numeric outcome, such as house price or albumin level. Logistic regression is used for a binary categorical outcome, such as sore throat after surgery coded yes/no or 1/0.

Identify the outcome and explore the data

First identify the outcome being measured or predicted and locate it in a data column. If it is not represented appropriately, the data may need cleaning or restructuring.
The outcome type informs the model choice. Predictors can be continuous or categorical; their type alone does not determine whether the model is linear or logistic.
Examine frequencies and visualizations before modeling. Imbalanced categories can make accuracy misleading: a model that predicts only the majority class could achieve 99% accuracy if 99 of 100 cases belong to that class, while failing to identify the minority cases of interest.
In the sore-throat example, predicting “no” for everyone could still be 75% correct. Check class balance and prediction patterns rather than relying on accuracy alone.
Ordered categories, such as disease stages, are sometimes treated as numbers even though they are not necessarily true numeric quantities. Consider whether that coding is appropriate.

Categorical predictors and reference categories

Categorical predictors need encoding because categories are not quantities with a meaningful one-unit increase. Dummy-variable encoding, also called one-hot encoding, is commonly used; tidy modeling tools can perform some of it automatically.
For a variable with (n) categories, the described approach creates (n-1) columns. Each column indicates membership in a category, and the all-zero pattern represents the omitted reference category.
In the housing example, condo is the reference for multifamily and residential. In the licorice-gargle example, sugar is the treatment reference; smoking categories are compared with never smokers.
Software may select a default reference, often the first factor level. Check the omitted category explicitly, especially when a variable has many levels, and change it when another comparison is more meaningful.
The reference choice changes the coefficients and their interpretation, not the underlying model fit. Data cleaning may be needed to set the intended labels and reference levels; consult the codebook when numeric codes or category names are unclear.

Choosing predictors

Predictors should be selected according to the research question and study design. Adding covariates gives the model additional coefficients and can change existing estimates because the model accounts for other factors.
Including variables indiscriminately can cause problems. Confounders and, in epidemiology, collider variables affect which predictors should be included; this is a research-design decision, not simply a matter of trying every available variable.
Data preparation continues during modeling, including encoding categorical variables. Automatic tools can help, but analysts need to understand the transformations being applied.




7. Linear regression fitting and interpretation

Fitting and extracting results

The Sacramento housing example predicts sale price from square footage and housing type. In base R, lm fits a linear model; the tidy-models approach provides an equivalent workflow.
Fitting produces a model object. The tidy function returns a data frame of model results, making coefficients easier to interpret, plot, or save as CSV or Excel.
A full statistical analysis may also consider p-values, confidence intervals, AIC, BIC, degrees of freedom, and other metadata; the coefficient examples focus on estimates.

Interpreting coefficients

A continuous-variable coefficient describes the expected outcome change for a one-unit increase in that predictor, holding other modeled variables constant. Confirm the variable’s units and transformations: one unit could mean an original measurement unit or, for a standardized variable, one standard deviation.
In the Sacramento example, the square-footage estimate is 139. Because square footage is untransformed, the model estimates a $139 increase in sale price for each additional square foot, holding other modeled variables constant.
Categorical coefficients compare each category with its reference category. With condo as the reference, the multifamily estimate is approximately (-$66{,}000), and the residential estimate is $8,253. These estimates describe price differences relative to condos at the same square footage.
The precise meaning of “multifamily” requires checking the data codebook.

Predictions and the intercept

Interpreting an individual coefficient is different from predicting an outcome. To predict, supply values for the case, multiply each predictor value by its coefficient, and add the terms and the intercept.
For example, a square-footage coefficient of 139 contributes 139,000 for a 1,000-square-foot house. A residential house also adds the residential coefficient of 8,253; the other terms and intercept are included in the prediction.
The intercept is the baseline prediction when all predictor values are zero. It is needed for prediction but may not have a useful real-world interpretation, such as for a zero-square-foot condo.




8. Logistic regression fitting and interpretation

Fitting binary-outcome models

Logistic regression is used for a two-category outcome. A multi-category outcome can be recoded as a binary outcome to address a specific question, such as cancer versus no cancer.
The model formula follows the general pattern used for linear regression, with the outcome on one side of the tilde and predictors on the other. In base R, use glm with family = binomial; the lecture also demonstrates tidy-model syntax.
Linear and logistic regression belong to the generalized linear model family. GLMs use a transformation appropriate to the outcome; Poisson models are another example in this family.

Log odds and odds ratios

A straight-line model can predict values below zero or above one, which are invalid probabilities for a binary outcome. Logistic regression uses a transformation to keep modeled values within the zero-to-one range.
Logistic-regression coefficients are on the log-odds scale, not direct probability changes. Odds are (P/(1-P)), so they are related to but distinct from probabilities.
Exponentiating a log-odds coefficient yields an odds ratio. For BMI in the sore-throat example, the coefficient is approximately (-0.0517); exponentiating it gives about 0.95. For each one-unit increase in BMI (one kilogram per meter squared), the odds of a sore throat are multiplied by 0.95, holding other variables constant.
In the treatment example, the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice are 0.38 times the odds for those who gargled sugar water. An example for sometimes or current smokers gives 4.38 times the odds compared with never smokers.
Describe these as odds, not probabilities. Odds ratios are commonly reported in epidemiology, including analyses based on two-by-two tables.
Categorical coefficients compare each level with the reference category. Changing the reference changes the comparison and coefficient values, but not the underlying model fit.

title: Lecture 2: Observational Units & Interpreting Regression Models
text:
Date Time: 2026-11-04
Instructor: Daniel Chen


This session bridged the gap between data cleaning and statistical modeling. It began by reinforcing the tidy data principle of observational units, demonstrating how to split a mixed dataset into separate, linked tables—a structure mirroring how hospital databases and health data standards like FHIR and OMOP organize patient records. The lecture then transitioned to fitting and interpreting linear and logistic regression models using the tidymodels package. Key concepts included dummy variable (one-hot) encoding for categorical predictors, selecting reference levels, and constructing human-readable interpretations for both continuous and categorical coefficients. For logistic regression, the instructor explained the log-odds transformation and how to convert coefficients into odds ratios. Finally, the session covered practical workflows for agentic coding in GitHub Codespaces, emphasizing strict data privacy protocols when using AI models with sensitive datasets and the importance of step-by-step code review.






Observational unit: The specific entity being observed (e.g., a song, a patient, a hospital visit). A core tidy data rule states that each type of observational unit should form its own separate table.

Splitting mixed tables: When a single table mixes multiple observational units (e.g., song metadata repeated for every week on a chart), extract the unique metadata rows, create a unique identifier (e.g., mutate(id = row_number())), and split it into its own table. Attach the id back to the measurement table using left_join(), then drop the redundant metadata columns.
Hospital data standards: Clinical databases follow this exact structure, with separate tables for patients, encounters, conditions, and medications, all linked by ID columns. Standards like HL7, FHIR, and the OMOP Common Data Model formalize this to allow secure, multi-site research without moving actual patient data.






Dummy variable encoding: Also called one-hot encoding in computer science. Regression models require numeric inputs, so categorical variables are automatically converted into 0/1 columns. For a categorical variable with \(k\) levels, \(k-1\) dummy columns are created.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Summary
Daniel Chen introduced a course sequence on data processing in R, covering data cleaning and transformation, visualization, modeling, and communicating results. The lectures emphasized tidy data: how to identify and reshape messy datasets, preserve information in analysis-ready form, and use Tidyverse tools for data manipulation and visualization. They also introduced regression and classification, linear regression interpretation, and an optional GitHub Codespaces environment with an AI coding agent.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Knowledge Points

1. Course structure, materials, and working environment

The course covers data cleaning and transformation, visualization, linear and logistic regression, and communicating results through reports. The instructor described the upcoming modeling material as planned for Thursday, November 5, and also referred to the next class as Wednesday, November 4, 2026; the schedule references were inconsistent.
Slides and related materials are available through the course website via Canvas. Students can read the slide content on the site or print it to PDF for annotation.
Suggested references include R for Data Science, material from UBC’s introductory data science course (DSI 100), and the instructor’s dissertation-based textbook for teaching data science to clinicians, which includes health-related datasets. The instructor recommended the 2014 tidy-data paper as a reference through section 4.
Students may use a GitHub Codespace to explore without installing or changing software on their own computers. The suggested setup is to create a GitHub account, sign up for the Student Pack, and start the Codespace from the course website’s Code option. Initial setup or a restart can take about 10 minutes. The Student Pack and Codespaces include free resources subject to usage limits.
The Codespace includes Copilot connected to an LLM and supports an agentic workflow: the agent can read files, write or edit code directly, and propose changes for the user to keep or reject. This can avoid copying code between tools, but generated changes must be reviewed; large edits can be difficult to manage. Do not put passwords or sensitive patient data in code or share identifiable records with an LLM. Generic code and column names can be used for visualization help without exposing row-level data.
The instructor presented AI tools as aids, not replacements for understanding and checking the work. Readable, maintainable code is preferable to dense code, including code generated by AI.



2. Tidy data: principles and diagnosing messy structures

Tidy data has three principles:

Each variable forms a column.
Each observation forms a row.
Each cell contains one value.

Data that has been collected or manually curated is not necessarily ready for analysis. A layout convenient for people to view may not preserve information or support reliable computer operations.
Hadley Wickham’s 2014 paper, Tidy Data, established the principles discussed in class. The instructor noted an earlier formulation concerning types and observational units, while emphasizing the one-value-per-cell principle in the lecture.
Useful signs that data may be messy include:

Column headers that encode values, such as years, income ranges, or weeks (WK1, WK2, etc.), rather than variable names.
A single column containing different kinds of measurements. For example, a count column mixing disease cases and population totals makes summaries such as means or maxima hard to interpret.
Column names that encode several variables, such as diagnosis, gender, and age in a name like m014.
Spreadsheet formatting—such as cell colors used to flag “good” or “bad”—that carries information not represented in the data itself. Such flags should be stored explicitly in a separate column.

Tidy data helps make filtering, grouping, calculations, and statistical summaries meaningful. The Tidyverse is a metapackage that loads several packages, including tidyr, which provides tools for tidying data.



3. Reshaping data with pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), and separate()

pivot_longer() gathers multiple columns into a longer format, placing former column headers in a key column and their contents in a value column. It is useful when headers encode values, such as income brackets or weekly rankings.
pivot_wider() turns unique values in a category column into separate columns, filling them with values from another column. It can separate different measurement types, such as minimum and maximum temperature.
These operations are conceptually similar to arranging fields in an Excel pivot table. Which one—or whether both—is needed depends on the dataset and the intended analysis.
Patterned columns can be selected by position, excluded with !, or matched by prefixes and other patterns. For example, columns beginning with WK can be gathered, and the prefix can be removed to leave the week number.
After removing a text prefix, convert numeric-looking values to numeric types. Otherwise, values may sort alphabetically (1, 10, 11, 2) rather than numerically.
separate() or pivot_longer() can split compound names into distinct variables. When curating data, delimiters such as underscores or dashes provide “breadcrumbs” that make automated separation more reliable.
If multiple observations share the same identifiers, include another variable to distinguish their source or context, such as the observer. Otherwise, software may aggregate or average duplicate observations unintentionally.


Examples discussed

Pew Research religion and income data: Income ranges appear as column headers alongside religion names. Pivoting longer makes it easier to group by religion, calculate totals, and filter or compare frequencies.
Billboard rankings: Weekly columns such as WK1 through WK70+ can be reshaped into fields for song information, week, and ranking. A song can then occupy multiple rows—one per chart week—and be analyzed by week or artist. Missing weeks or rankings can be handled during the transformation.
WHO tuberculosis and census data: Headers may compress demographics or diagnosis details. Separating them into fields such as diagnosis, gender, age, and count makes demographic aggregation more direct.
Antarctic expedition measurements: Records by location and date can contain missing minimum or maximum temperature readings, which require explicit handling.




4. Data storage, formats, and missing values

Relational databases divide complex institutional data, such as hospital records, among specialized tables for patients, encounters, and procedures. Linking records with identifiers such as Patient ID avoids repeatedly storing the same demographic information.
CSV files are widely usable for data exchange and tutorials because they do not require proprietary software. Excel files are common in ad hoc workflows and can be read in R with packages such as readxl; enterprise systems generally use other data infrastructure.
Spreadsheet layouts that put time-series observations in columns can encounter software column limits. The lecture cited an NHS COVID-19 tracking failure in which daily counts arranged across columns exceeded a spreadsheet limit, leading to lost or overwritten data and disrupted predictive models.
In R, actual missing values are represented by NA, distinct from empty strings or special codes such as 99. is.na() returns logical values; because TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, summing is.na(column) counts missing values, while summing !is.na(column) counts non-missing values.



5. Tidyverse data manipulation

select() chooses columns, while filter() chooses rows that satisfy conditions. Columns can be selected by name or pattern—for example, names beginning with bill, ending in _text, or within a range such as Q21 through Q47. Multiple selections can be combined.
filter() conditions can use comparisons and logical operators. Use == to test equality; a single = is used for assignment or naming arguments. ! negates a condition, and | represents logical OR. Conditions can also be combined to require multiple criteria.
mutate() creates or transforms columns. For example, body mass in grams can be converted to kilograms by dividing by 1,000. For recoding or type conversion, creating an intermediate column can make it easier to verify the result before dropping the original with select().
The base R pipe, |> (available from R 4.0), chains operations in sequence and can replace the Tidyverse pipe %>%. It supports readable, vertically arranged workflows such as mutating, filtering, and selecting in order.
group_by() partitions data by one or more variables, and summarize() calculates statistics for each group. Summary functions include mean(), median(), min(), max(), and n(); multiple summaries can be produced in one call.



6. Dates and the Palmer Penguins dataset

When day values are spread across patterned columns, use pivot_longer() to gather them, extract the day from the column name, remove prefixes, convert the day to an integer, and retain the corresponding measurement.
Separate minimum and maximum measurements into distinct columns when a combined value column would make averages or extrema ambiguous.
Combine year, month, and day into a proper date or timestamp before date arithmetic. Computers can then calculate intervals between dates; time zones also need appropriate handling.
The Palmer Penguins dataset was used as a practice example. It contains 344 observations and eight columns, including species, island, sex, year, bill and flipper measurements, and body mass.
A two-step transformation can be easier to read and debug than a compact nested operation. Small differences in computing time are generally less important than code that can be understood and checked.



7. Visualization with ggplot2

ggplot2 expects tidy data. The aes() function maps columns to plot properties such as the x-axis, y-axis, and color; plots are built by adding layers with +.
Suitable basic plots depend on variable types:

Two continuous variables: scatter plot with geom_point().
One continuous variable: histogram.
Categorical variables: bar chart, which may be stacked or dodged.

geom_bar() uses stat = "count" to count observations for a categorical variable. geom_col() uses stat = "identity" and requires precomputed y-values. Use geom_col() when a summary table already contains counts or frequencies.
Labels, themes, and other styling can be added as layers.



8. Modeling: prediction targets and linear regression

A model needs clearly identified columns for its target and inputs. Inputs may be called predictors, independent variables, or Xs; the target may be called the response, dependent variable, or Y. Data cleaning and column selection can occur at different stages, and data work is iterative.
The target’s type determines the general prediction task:

A numeric target calls for regression, such as predicting age, an albumin score, or house price.
A categorical target calls for classification, such as predicting survival, disease status, or disease stage. Binary outcomes are common introductory examples.

In an R formula, the tilde separates the target from predictors: the target is on the left, and input variables are on the right. Predictors do not all need to be numeric; for example, a categorical variable can help predict a numeric outcome.
Visualize relationships before modeling when practical. A scatter plot can show the relationship between two numeric variables, though a model can include more predictors than can be displayed in a simple plot.
Linear regression models numeric outcomes. Its formula relates to y = mx + b: the target is y, predictors correspond to x terms, and coefficients represent slopes, with an intercept term. With multiple predictors, the model includes a coefficient for each.
In the Sacramento housing example, a coefficient of 138.5 for square footage indicates an expected increase of $138.50 in house price per additional square foot. Linear and logistic regression are commonly used in biostatistics partly because their results can often be described in interpretable terms. Logistic regression for categorical outcomes was introduced as upcoming material.



9. Course logistics

A session break was called for 2:08 PM on November 2, 2026. The lecture was recorded, and the course site was expected to include an audio transcript and AI-generated summary.
The instructor noted classroom display and Zoom setup issues. He also described having gone to the wrong building after misreading an invitation; the recording does not establish the intended venue.

title: Tidy Data, Wrangling, and First Modelling
text:
Date Time: 2026-11-02 13:00:00
Location: ECC 100 LT
Instructor: Daniel Chen


Session 1 introduced the foundational principles of data cleaning and manipulation in R using the tidyverse ecosystem. The instructor defined “tidy data” as a standardized format where each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value is a single cell. Students learned to identify common violations of these rules—such as column headers containing values, multiple variables packed into one column, and variables split across rows and columns—and practiced reshaping messy datasets into tidy formats using pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().
After establishing tidy data, the lecture covered core data wrangling operations with dplyr. The class practiced selecting columns, filtering rows, and creating new variables with mutate(), emphasizing the pipe operator (|>) for chaining steps cleanly without creating intermediate variables. The session then transitioned to exploratory data visualization with ggplot2, demonstrating how to map variables to geometric objects like scatter plots, histograms, and bar charts based on their data types.
Finally, the instructor provided a first look at statistical modelling, explaining how tidy data enables clear model specification. Using a linear regression example, the class learned to fit a model, interpret the slope coefficient as a rate of change, and use the tidymodels framework (recipe, workflow, fit) to standardize the modelling pipeline. The session concluded with a demonstration of GitHub Copilot in Codespaces, showing how agentic AI can edit code directly to streamline the workflow.






Tidy data: A consistent data structure that makes analysis, visualization, and modelling straightforward. Defined by three rules: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each value is a cell.
Column headers as values: When column names (e.g., income brackets, years, weeks) actually represent levels of a variable, the dataset violates tidy principles. Resolved by pivoting wide to long.
Multiple variables in one column: When a single cell or header contains embedded information (e.g., sp_m_014 for diagnosis, gender, and age). Resolved by splitting headers or using separate().
Variables in rows and columns: When multiple variables (e.g., tmax and tmin) are stacked in rows while other dimensions (e.g., days) are spread across columns. Requires both pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().





pivot_longer(): Converts wide-format data into long-format data. Useful when values are spread across column headers. Key arguments include cols (which columns to pivot), names_to (new column for headers), and values_to (new column for values).
pivot_wider(): Converts long-format data into wide-format data. Useful when variables are stacked in rows and need to become separate columns. Uses names_from and values_from.
names_prefix / names_transform: Arguments in pivot_longer() to strip text prefixes from column names and immediately convert types (e.g., as.integer) during the pivot, avoiding messy strings.
values_drop_na = TRUE: Drops missing values during pivoting to keep the resulting dataset cleaner and avoid empty rows.





select(): Chooses specific columns to retain. Can use exact names or helper functions like starts_with() or ends_with().
filter(): Subsets rows based on logical conditions (>, <, ==, !=, &, |). Returns only rows where the condition evaluates to TRUE.
mutate(): Adds new columns or modifies existing ones. Does not alter the original dataset; output must be assigned to a new variable or piped forward.
group_by(): Groups the dataset by a categorical variable so that subsequent functions apply calculations to each group independently.
summarize(): Computes a single summary value (e.g., mean(), max(), n()) for each group. Requires na.rm = TRUE when calculating means or sums with missing values.
|> (pipe operator): Passes the result of the expression on its left as the first argument to the function on its right. Enables linear, readable chaining of operations.





ggplot(): Initializes a plot by mapping the dataset and aesthetic variables (aes()), which link columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill).
geom_point(): Creates scatter plots for two continuous/quantitative variables.
geom_histogram(): Creates histograms for one continuous variable, binning the data to show distribution.
geom_bar(): Creates bar charts for categorical variables. Automatically counts occurrences (stat = "count").
geom_col(): Creates bar charts when the counts are already calculated in the data (stat = "identity"), requiring explicit y mapping.
labs(): Adds human-readable titles, axis labels, and legend titles to polish the figure.





Outcome variable types: Dictates the modelling approach. Continuous outcomes (numbers) use regression; categorical outcomes (groups/labels) use classification.
Model formula: Uses the tilde (~) to separate predictors from the outcome. The variable on the left is what you predict; variables on the right are inputs.
Linear regression: Fits a straight line (\(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)). The slope coefficient (β₁) represents the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in the predictor. Highly interpretable in clinical/medical contexts.
tidymodels workflow: Uses recipe() to define preprocessing, linear_reg()/logistic_reg() to define the model, and workflow() + fit() to train it. Standardizes the modelling pipeline.







# Pew survey: pivot wide income columns into long rows
pew_tidy <- pew |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -religion,
    names_to = "income",
    values_to = "frequency"
  )
# Billboard chart: pivot week columns, drop "wk" prefix, convert to integer
billboard_tidy <- billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |>
  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)
# WHO TB data: pivot all non-ID columns, split header on "_" into 3 new variables
who2 |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !(country:year),
    names_to = c("diagnosis", "gender", "age"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "count",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
# Weather data: pivot days to long, make dates, pivot temp types to wide
weather_tidy <- weather |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("d"),
    names_to = "day",
    names_prefix = "d",
    names_transform = list(day = as.integer),
    values_to = "temp",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = element,
    values_from = temp
  ) |>
  select(id, date, tmax, tmin) |>
  arrange(id, date)



# Chain select, mutate, filter using the pipe
penguins |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000) |>
  filter(flipper_len > 190) |>
  select(species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg)
# Group by species and calculate average body mass
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(avg_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE))
The pipe (|>) passes the output of the left side directly as the first argument to the function on the right. This allows you to read the code chronologically (“and then…”) and avoids cluttering the environment with intermediate data frames.



# Scatter plot of flipper length vs body mass
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

# Add colour by species and custom axis labels
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )
ggplot2 uses a layering system. You map data to aesthetics inside aes(), then add geometric layers (geom_) with +. Colour and fill map categorical variables to visual distinctions.



# Specify recipe, model specification, and fit workflow
house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)
# View the fitted model coefficients
tidy(house_fit)
The recipe() function defines the mathematical relationship (price ~ sqft). The workflow() combines preprocessing and model definition, and fit() trains it. The coefficient table shows an intercept of ~13,859 and a slope of ~138.5, meaning each additional square foot increases the predicted house price by $138.50.




Codespace restart times & monitor setup: The instructor spent the first few minutes troubleshooting Zoom screen sharing and realizing he was looking at the wrong monitor. He noted that if a Codespace times out or is accidentally closed, it takes several minutes to rebuild and install dependencies, so leaving it running is recommended.
Excel visual flags vs. computer parsing: A student asked how computers handle Excel cells formatted with colours to indicate status. The instructor explained that R and other data tools do not read cell background colours; visual flags must be explicitly converted into a new column to be analyzable.






Q: What is the practical difference between geom_bar() and geom_col()? A: geom_bar() automatically counts the occurrences of categories in a single column (stat = "count"). geom_col() assumes the counts are already calculated in the dataset and draws bars based on the provided y-values (stat = "identity"). Use geom_col() when you’ve already summarized your data.
Q: How does the LLM agent in GitHub Codespaces work compared to a standard chatbot? A: Unlike web chat interfaces that just return text to copy-paste, the agent in the Codespace reads your actual project files and can edit them directly. You can ask it to “make a plot from the patients data” and it will generate and save the code in your script, which you then review and accept. This shifts the workflow from typing from scratch to reviewing and verifying AI-generated code.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
You are taking notes for a graduate student in UBC’s Experimental Medicine program who has not coded before, for the course MEDI 504A (Emerging Topics in Experimental Medicine), in the two sessions Daniel Chen teaches on biostatistics with the tidyverse.
Session 1 is a lecture on tidy data: reshaping with tidyr (pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), separate()), wrangling with dplyr, plotting with ggplot2, and a first look at modelling. Session 2 is a lab: tidying medical datasets from the medicaldata package, then linear and logistic regression with tidymodels, leading into a homework assignment. Students work in R and Quarto, in a GitHub Codespace with GitHub Copilot or on their own computer.
Using LLMs is taught in a later part of the course, by another instructor; these sessions don’t cover statistical theory beyond reading and interpreting the models.
You will receive up to two inputs describing a single session. Turn them into notes a student can revise from weeks later, when they no longer remember it.
The instructor live-codes from the slides, so the slides are this course’s record of what was typed and what came back. They are what separate these notes from a generic summary. The transcript tells you what was explained and what students asked; the slides give the exact code and its output. Work from both. When the slides are absent, work from the transcript alone and omit whatever you cannot support.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Output format
Produce a Markdown document with exactly these parts, in this order. Omit any section the inputs give you nothing real for — never emit a placeholder.
# <Short title naming the session's main topic>

Date Time: <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, if stated or inferable; otherwise omit this line>
Location: <only if actually stated; otherwise omit this line>
Instructor: <speaker who is clearly teaching>

## Summary

Two to four paragraphs of prose covering what the session was about and what
changed for the student as a result. No bullets here.

## Knowledge Points

### 1. <Theme>
- **<Term>**: explanation.
  - nested detail where a term has parts worth separating

### 2. <Theme>
...

## Code from class

### [<What was being done>](<the slide's link from the course materials>)

```r
code                     # what it was for
```

A line or two of prose after a block, where the sequence needs explaining.

### What went wrong live

- **<What broke>**: what happened, and what fixed it.

## Questions

- **Q:** a question a student actually asked.
  **A:** how the instructor answered it.

## Also on the slides

- [<Slide heading>](<its link>): one line on what it shows.

## Assignments

- [ ] Task, with its due date.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Rules
Ground everything in the inputs. Every function, argument, due date, tool name and claim must be traceable to something actually said or shown on the slides. If the transcript is garbled or ambiguous on a detail and the slides don’t settle it, leave the detail out rather than guessing at it. Never invent a plausible-sounding due date, argument, or URL.
Write functions, arguments, column names, file names and code as inline code — pivot_longer(), names_to = "week", body_mass, data/pew.csv, |>. When a function is described but not named, name it.
Use absolute dates. The transcript says “see you Wednesday”; the notes say “Wednesday, 2026-11-04”. Anchor to the lecture date. If you cannot work out the real calendar date, write the weekday alone rather than an invented date.
Protect student privacy. The transcript anonymises students as Speaker 2, Speaker 4, and so on. Never invent a name for them and never carry a student’s name through even if one is spoken aloud. Attribute questions generically — “a student asked”. The instructor may be named.
Preserve warnings as warnings. When the instructor flags something as dangerous, irreversible, or a common mistake, say so in the notes with the same force. Never put a password or identifiable patient data in your code or in a prompt to an LLM; that has to survive into the notes.
Capture the questions properly. These are the highest-value part of the notes, because they are what a generic summariser misses. Include questions asked mid-lecture, not only ones at the end, and include the answer. Cover troubleshooting exchanges — a student describing a Codespace that won’t start and the instructor working through it is a question.
Repair transcription noise silently. Machine transcripts mangle technical terms: “DSi one hundred” is DSCI 100, “R for DS” is R for Data Science, “percent greater percent” is %>%, “vertical pipe greater than” is |>, “pivot longer” is pivot_longer(), “group by” is group_by(), “geombar” is geom_bar(), “geom_scatter” is geom_point(), and “code space” is a GitHub Codespace. Fix these without commenting on them. Drop filler, false starts, and pure classroom logistics (“give me one second”) unless they carry content.
Be complete over brief. A student who missed the lecture should be able to follow along. Prefer a ## Knowledge Points section that runs long to one that drops a topic the instructor spent ten minutes on.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Rules for the slides
The slides are the authority on code. A transcript renders pivot_longer() as “pivot longer” and drops arguments entirely. Where the slides and the transcript disagree about a function, an argument, a column or a file name, the slides are right — everywhere in the notes, not only in ## Code from class. Where the slides give an exact column name, path, or value, use it in place of a vague one from the transcript.
Never invent code. Everything in ## Code from class must appear in <course-materials>, or be spoken clearly enough in the transcript to be unambiguous. If the slides are absent, omit ## Code from class entirely rather than reconstructing it from what such a lecture usually covers.
Follow the class, not the deck. The slides can hold more than the class got through, and the instructor can skip around. Use the transcript to decide what was taught, and in what order. Write up what was taught. List slide sections the transcript never reaches under ## Also on the slides, one line each, rather than writing them up as taught.
Group the code by what was being done, in the order it happened. One ### per task — tidying the Billboard chart, counting missing values — not one per function. Keep the slides’ order inside a block, and comment the lines whose purpose is not obvious from the code itself. Someone should be able to work down the section and reproduce the session.
Link back to the slides. Each heading in <course-materials> carries the link to its section on the website. Link a ### in ## Code from class to the slide it came from, and link the entries in ## Also on the slides. Use those links exactly as given; never build or guess a URL.
Quote real output only where it teaches. The slides hold far more output than belongs in notes. Quote it when the output is the lesson — the shape of a table before and after pivot_longer(), the column types read_csv() reports, a coefficient being interpreted. Quote verbatim, in a fenced block, trimmed to the lines that matter. Never quote pages of routine output.
Use the transcript for what went wrong. The slides show code that worked. A live error, a typo the instructor fixed, or a question that exposed a misunderstanding comes from the transcript; put it in ### What went wrong live with what resolved it. If nothing went wrong, omit that subsection.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Output discipline
Output only the Markdown document. No preamble, no “Here are the notes”, no commentary afterwards, and do not wrap the whole document in a code fence.
Do not write a provenance footer or a trailing --- separator. The generator appends that automatically.

title: AI Class Notes
text:
We record each class and post its transcript and notes on this site. In the course repository, they’re in the sessions/ folder, with one folder per class named by its date.
AI models write the notes from the transcript and the slides, so they can get things wrong. Check anything important against the slides. We ran the same prompt through more than one model, so you can compare their notes with each other and with the notes Plaud, the recording app, makes on its own. To see how the notes are made, or to suggest a change to the prompt, read How the notes are made.

title: Solutions: Extra practice: logistic regression
text:
Note



These are the solutions to the Extra practice: logistic regression exercises. Try each exercise yourself before you look.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)
We make blood and cmv the same way as the exercise page.
blood <- blood_storage |>
  mutate(
    recurrence = factor(Recurrence, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    rbc_age_group = factor(RBC.Age.Group, levels = 1:3,
                           labels = c("younger", "middle", "older"))
  )

cmv <- cytomegalovirus |>
  mutate(
    cmv = factor(cmv, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    recipient.cmv = factor(recipient.cmv, levels = c(0, 1),
                           labels = c("negative", "positive")),
    donor.cmv = factor(donor.cmv, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("negative", "positive"))
  )

title: Solutions: Extra practice: logistic regression
section: Exercise 4: What does this model ignore?
text:
Exercise 4: What does this model ignore?
Time. The men were followed for different lengths of time (TimeToRecurrence), and some left the study before a recurrence could be seen (Censor). Logistic regression only asks whether recurrence happened. Survival analysis, which the original study used, also models when.

  fit(cmv ~ donor.cmv + recipient.cmv + time.to.transplant, data = cmv)

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Back to Sacramento
On Monday we fit price ~ sqft on the Sacramento house sales. Let’s add type, a categorical variable, so we can see how to read both kinds of variables.

Sacramento |>
  count(type)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  type             n
  <fct>        <int>
1 Condo           53
2 Multi_Family    13
3 Residential    866

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Dummy variables

A regression needs numbers, so R turns a categorical variable (a factor) into dummy variables, also called indicator variables
Each dummy variable is a 0/1 column for one level, and there’s one for every level except the first
The level without a column is the reference level, and every other level gets compared with it

title: Interpreting a linear regression
section: Two names for the same idea
text:
Two names for the same idea

Statistics calls this dummy variable encoding
Computer science and machine learning call it one-hot encoding
Both turn each level of a categorical variable into a 0/1 column
One-hot encoding usually keeps a column for every level, while a regression with an intercept drops one, the reference level (R does this for us)

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
type as dummy variables
type has 3 levels, so it becomes 2 dummy variables, with Condo as the reference:



type
typeMulti_Family
typeResidential




Condo
0
0


Multi_Family
1
0


Residential
0
1

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Fit the model

house_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento)

house_tidy <- tidy(house_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
house_tidy

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term             estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         6885.  12169.       0.566 5.72e-  1  -16996.    30766.
2 sqft                 139.      3.88    35.7   1.64e-176     131.      146.
3 typeMulti_Family  -66224.  26222.      -2.53  1.17e-  2 -117686.   -14762.
4 typeResidential     8253.  12151.       0.679 4.97e-  1  -15594.    32100.



One row for sqft
One row for each dummy variable, and no row for Condo, the reference level

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Interpreting a continuous variable

For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect [outcome] to increase (or decrease) by [estimate] [units], all else remaining the same.

For sqft:

For every 1 square foot increase in size, we expect the sale price to increase by $139, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $131 to $146).


“All else remaining the same” means the other variables in the model, so here, a house of the same type

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Interpreting a categorical variable

We expect [outcome] for [level] to be [estimate] [units] higher (or lower) than for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For typeMulti_Family:

We expect multi-family homes to sell for $66,224 less than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $14,762 to $117,686 less).


Here “all else” is the size: a multi-family home and a condo with the same square footage
The comparison is always with the reference level, Condo

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
When the interval includes 0
For typeResidential:

We expect residential homes to sell for $8,253 more than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: -$15,594 to $32,100).


The interval includes 0, so the data don’t show a clear difference between residential homes and condos of the same size
We still report the estimate and its interval, and say that it’s unclear

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
The intercept

The intercept is the expected outcome when every continuous variable is 0 and every categorical variable is at its reference level
Here that’s a condo with 0 square feet, which doesn’t exist, so we don’t interpret it

title: Interpreting a linear regression
section: The same model in base R
text:
The same model in base R
Base R’s lm() fits the same model with less code:

lm(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento) |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term             estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         6885.  12169.       0.566 5.72e-  1  -16996.    30766.
2 sqft                 139.      3.88    35.7   1.64e-176     131.      146.
3 typeMulti_Family  -66224.  26222.      -2.53  1.17e-  2 -117686.   -14762.
4 typeResidential     8253.  12151.       0.679 4.97e-  1  -15594.    32100.



The same estimates and intervals as linear_reg()
We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps
