title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
A sore throat after surgery
licorice_gargle (from medicaldata) is a trial of 235 adults having thoracic surgery with a large breathing tube. Before the tube went in, they were randomized to gargle licorice or sugar water. Our outcome is any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Recode the variables

sore <- licorice_gargle |>
  mutate(
    sore_throat = factor(pacu30min_throatPain > 0,
                         levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("no", "yes")),
    treatment = factor(treat, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("sugar", "licorice")),
    smoking = factor(preOp_smoking, levels = c(3, 2, 1),
                     labels = c("never", "past",
                                "current"))
  ) |>
  select(sore_throat, treatment,
         bmi = preOp_calcBMI, smoking) |>
  drop_na()

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Which level are we modelling?

logistic_reg() models the odds of the outcome’s second level
sore_throat has the levels no, then yes, so every result is about the odds of a sore throat
The predictors are a mix of both kinds:

treatment: 2 levels, so 1 dummy variable (reference sugar)
bmi: continuous, in kg/m²
smoking: 3 levels, so 2 dummy variables (reference never)



count(sore, sore_throat)

  sore_throat   n
1          no 169
2         yes  64

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Fit the model

sore_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
      data = sore)

tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         0.0240    0.979     0.0245 0.980      -1.91     1.95  
2 treatmentlicorice  -0.956     0.316    -3.02   0.00252    -1.59    -0.346 
3 bmi                -0.0517    0.0385   -1.34   0.179      -0.129    0.0229
4 smokingpast         1.48      0.428     3.45   0.000551    0.664    2.35  
5 smokingcurrent      0.635     0.410     1.55   0.121      -0.152    1.46  



These estimates are on the log-odds scale, \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)\), which is hard to read

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Exponentiate to get odds ratios

sore_or <- sore_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
sore_or

  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 



exponentiate = TRUE turns each estimate and its interval into an odds ratio (std.error, statistic, and p.value stay on the log-odds scale)
An odds ratio of 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower odds, and above 1 means higher odds

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Interpreting a continuous variable

For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio], all else remaining the same.

For bmi:

For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI, we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by 0.95, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.88 to 1.02).


Multiplied by 0.95 is the same as 5% lower odds
The interval includes 1, so the data don’t show a clear effect of BMI

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Interpreting a categorical variable

We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level] to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For treatmentlicorice:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice to be 0.38 times the odds for patients who gargled sugar water, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.71).


That’s 62% lower odds, and the interval doesn’t include 1

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
section: A categorical variable with more levels
text:
A categorical variable with more levels
Each dummy variable compares one level with the reference, never. For smokingpast:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for past smokers to be 4.38 times the odds for people who never smoked, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 1.94 to 10.48).


smokingcurrent compares current smokers with people who never smoked, not with past smokers
Its interval (0.86 to 4.33) includes 1, so that comparison isn’t clear

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Odds, not probability

An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities
Say “0.38 times the odds”, not “0.38 times as likely” or “62% less likely”
The two are close only when the outcome is rare, and here 27% of patients had a sore throat

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
section: The same model in base R
text:
The same model in base R
Base R’s glm() fits the same model with less code:

glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
    family = binomial, data = sore) |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02

family = binomial is what makes glm() a logistic regression
The same odds ratios and intervals as logistic_reg()
We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Exercise 1: Fit a logistic regression
Logistic regression models the log-odds of the event:
\[
\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \dots
\]
where \(p\) is the probability of recurrence. Exponentiating a coefficient, \(e^{\beta}\), gives an odds ratio.






NoteYour turn




Before we model, let’s look at the outcome. Plot the proportion of men with a recurrence in each storage-age group as stacked bars (geom_bar(position = "fill")). Does recurrence look different between the groups?
Fit a logistic regression of recurrence on rbc_age_group.
Show the odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
What group are the odds ratios compared with? Is older stored blood associated with recurrence?


ggplot(blood, aes(x = ____, fill = ____)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")

rec_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(____ ~ ____, data = blood)

tidy(rec_fit, exponentiate = ____, conf.int = ____)

title: Observational units
text:
The original third rule
The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

title: Observational units
section: Problem 5: one unit in many tables
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables
The opposite problem is one kind of observation split across many files, such as one file per year or one per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them with bind_rows() or give read_csv() all the file names at once.

title: Observational units
text:
How hospitals store data
Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule, with one table per kind of observational unit, linked by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake but realistic patient records stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients in CSV, HL7 FHIR, and C-CDA formats.

title: Observational units
text:
Beyond CSVs: health data standards
In practice, health data is usually stored and shared using data standards, not as a folder of CSV files.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, which sends a patient, an encounter, or an observation as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on many hospitals’ databases

All of these follow the third rule, with one table (or resource) per kind of observational unit, linked by IDs.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Visualization: ask a question, then answer it
text:
Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

When we make a plot, we’re trying to answer a question about our data, and a good plot answers it clearly.


Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
ggplot2: three parts
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill)
Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them (geom_point(), geom_histogram(), geom_bar())
Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer with +.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Scatter plot: two quantitative variables
Is a penguin’s body mass related to its flipper length?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Add colour and labels

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Histogram: one quantitative variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable
text:
Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Rules of thumb

Answer one question per plot
Label axes, with units
Use colourblind-friendly palettes
Avoid pie charts, 3D, and tables of numbers when a plot will do

title: Wrangling and visualizing

Data wrangling

Real-world data is usually messy. Once it’s in a tidy “shape”, we only need a few dplyr functions for most of our work.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
The Palmer penguins
This dataset has 344 penguins of 3 species, collected from 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica. It’s been built into R since version 4.5. We’ll convert it into a tibble so it prints nicely.

penguins <- as_tibble(penguins)

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
mutate(): add or change columns
Body mass is in grams, so let’s add a column with the mass in kilograms.

mutate(penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000)

# A tibble: 344 × 9
   species island    bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex     year
   <fct>   <fct>        <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct>  <int>
 1 Adelie  Torgersen     39.1     18.7         181      3750 male    2007
 2 Adelie  Torgersen     39.5     17.4         186      3800 female  2007
 3 Adelie  Torgersen     40.3     18           195      3250 female  2007
 4 Adelie  Torgersen     NA       NA            NA        NA <NA>    2007
 5 Adelie  Torgersen     36.7     19.3         193      3450 female  2007
 6 Adelie  Torgersen     39.3     20.6         190      3650 male    2007
 7 Adelie  Torgersen     38.9     17.8         181      3625 female  2007
 8 Adelie  Torgersen     39.2     19.6         195      4675 male    2007
 9 Adelie  Torgersen     34.1     18.1         193      3475 <NA>    2007
10 Adelie  Torgersen     42       20.2         190      4250 <NA>    2007
# ℹ 334 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: body_mass_kg <dbl>


mutate() gives back a new data frame and doesn’t change penguins. If we want to keep the result, we need to assign it (<-) to a variable.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Doing many steps at once
We can save each step as its own object,

penguins_1 <- mutate(penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000)
penguins_2 <- filter(penguins_1, flipper_len > 190)
penguins_3 <- select(penguins_2, species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg)

or we can nest the function calls, but then we have to read them from the inside out.

penguins_nested <- select(
  filter(mutate(penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000), flipper_len > 190),
  species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg
)

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
The pipe, |>
The pipe takes whatever is on its left and passes it in as the first argument of the function on its right. We can read each |> as “and then”.

penguins |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000) |>
  filter(flipper_len > 190) |>
  select(species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg)

# A tibble: 243 × 3
   species flipper_len body_mass_kg
   <fct>         <int>        <dbl>
 1 Adelie          195         3.25
 2 Adelie          193         3.45
 3 Adelie          195         4.68
 4 Adelie          193         3.48
 5 Adelie          191         3.8 
 6 Adelie          198         4.4 
 7 Adelie          195         3.45
 8 Adelie          197         4.5 
 9 Adelie          194         4.2 
10 Adelie          195         3.32

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
group_by() and summarize()
group_by() splits the data into groups, and summarize() calculates a single value for each group.

penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(avg_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   avg_body_mass
  <fct>             <dbl>
1 Adelie            3701.
2 Chinstrap         3733.
3 Gentoo            5076.


We need na.rm = TRUE to skip the missing values. Otherwise, a single NA makes the whole mean NA.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
How many values are missing?

penguins |>
  summarize(n = n(), missing_body_mass = sum(is.na(body_mass)))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
      n missing_body_mass
  <int>             <int>
1   344                 2



penguins |>
  count(species, island)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  species   island        n
  <fct>     <fct>     <int>
1 Adelie    Biscoe       44
2 Adelie    Dream        56
3 Adelie    Torgersen    52
4 Chinstrap Dream        68
5 Gentoo    Biscoe      124

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Visualization: ask a question, then answer it
text:
Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

When we make a plot, we’re trying to answer a question about our data, and a good plot answers it clearly.


Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
ggplot2: three parts
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill)
Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them (geom_point(), geom_histogram(), geom_bar())
Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer with +.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Scatter plot: two quantitative variables
Is a penguin’s body mass related to its flipper length?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Add colour and labels

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Histogram: one quantitative variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable
text:
Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Rules of thumb

Answer one question per plot
Label axes, with units
Use colourblind-friendly palettes
Avoid pie charts, 3D, and tables of numbers when a plot will do

text: You can follow along in a Codespace with nothing to install, and it’s where you can use GitHub Copilot for the homework. To work on your own computer instead, install everything below before Lecture 2. None of it needs AI tools.

title: Local setup
text:
A GitHub account
In Lecture 2 you’ll make your own copy (a fork) of the course repository, so you’ll need a free GitHub account: https://github.com/signup.

title: Local setup
text:
R
Install R 4.5 or newer from CRAN: https://cloud.r-project.org/. Lecture 1 uses the penguins data built into R since version 4.5.

title: Local setup
text:
An editor
Use either of these:

Positron: https://positron.posit.co/
RStudio Desktop: https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/

title: Local setup
text:
Quarto 1.10 or newer
Install Quarto from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/, even if your editor came with its own copy. The course website’s theme needs Quarto 1.10 or newer, and the copy that comes with Positron or RStudio is usually older. With an older Quarto, rendering stops with an error that says the “UBC brand” extension “is incompatible with this quarto version”.
After you install it, restart your editor, open its terminal, and run:

Terminal
quarto --version

It should print 1.10 or a higher number.
Quarto also makes the homework’s PDF, using Typst, so you don’t need to install LaTeX.

title: Local setup
text:
R packages
Run this once in the R console:
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse", "tidymodels", "medicaldata", "knitr", "rmarkdown"
))
Quarto uses knitr and rmarkdown to run the R code in a document.

title: Local setup
text:
Git
You’ll clone your fork in Lecture 2. Install Git by following Happy Git and GitHub for the useR: https://happygitwithr.com/install-git.html.

Once you’ve cloned your fork in Lecture 2, open example.qmd and render it, as the Clone the repository page shows. If it renders, everything you need is installed. If you use RStudio, also follow that page’s tip on running chunks from the top folder.

UBC MEDI 504A (Emerging Topics in Experimental Medicine), 2026 Winter 1 term. These are the two lectures for week 2 of the course, on basic biostatistics. We start with tidy data, then fit linear and logistic regression models on medical data.

text:
A first look at the data
data/patients.csv is a small practice dataset of 12 synthetic patients, from ehsanx/HDSx-workspace. The code chunk below reads it and shows the first few rows.

patients <- read.csv("data/patients.csv")

title: Tidy data
text:
What is tidy data?


Each variable is a column; each column is a variable
Each observation is a row; each row is an observation
Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value



Rules from R for Data Science (2e), chapter 5. Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst, from the Openscapes blog (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
The original definition (2014)
The Tidy Data paper defines it a little differently:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

The third rule is really about databases, where data is split into separate tables and joined back together. The newer definition replaces it with “each value is a cell”. We’ll come back to observational units in Lecture 2’s Observational units section.

title: Tidy data
text:
Why bother?

Once our data is tidy, we can use the same tools every time we summarize, plot, or model it.


Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
Five ways data gets messy
From the Tidy Data paper:

Column headers are values, not variable names
Multiple variables are stored in one column
Variables are stored in both rows and columns
Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

We’ll go through the first three using the datasets from the paper. Problems 4 and 5 are about observational units, which we’ll cover in Lecture 2’s Observational units section.

  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",

  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)

  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("d"),
    names_to = "day",

    values_drop_na = TRUE

  mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = element, # tmax and tmin become their own columns
    values_from = temp

  select(id, date, tmax, tmin) |>
  arrange(id, date)

Function

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Two kinds of questions
When we want to predict something, the type of outcome tells us what kind of model to use.

Regression, when the outcome is quantitative. What will this house sell for? How heavy will this baby be at birth?
Classification, when the outcome is categorical. Will this patient’s cancer come back, yes or no?

Today we’ll fit a linear regression. On Wednesday we’ll fit linear and logistic regressions on medical data.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Models need tidy data
A model formula like price ~ sqft expects the data to have one row per observation (each house sale) and one column per variable (the price and the size), which is what tidy data gives us.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Is size related to price?

ggplot(Sacramento, aes(x = sqft, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "House size (square feet)", y = "Sale price (USD)")

title: From tidy data to models
section: Linear regression: the line of best fit
text:
Linear regression: the line of best fit
\[
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The “best” line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances between the line and the data points.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Fit it with tidymodels

house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)
house_fit

title: From tidy data to models
text:
More than one predictor
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_m X_m
\]
To use more predictors, we add them to the formula.

recipe(price ~ sqft + beds + baths, data = Sacramento)




── Recipe ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────





── Inputs 


Number of variables by role


outcome:   1
predictor: 3


Now each slope is how much the outcome changes for one predictor, when the other predictors stay the same.

title: Tidy data
text:
Why bother?

Once our data is tidy, we can use the same tools every time we summarize, plot, or model it.


Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
Five ways data gets messy
From the Tidy Data paper:

Column headers are values, not variable names
Multiple variables are stored in one column
Variables are stored in both rows and columns
Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

We’ll go through the first three using the datasets from the paper. Problems 4 and 5 are about observational units, which we’ll cover in Lecture 2’s Observational units section.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Two kinds of questions
When we want to predict something, the type of outcome tells us what kind of model to use.

Regression, when the outcome is quantitative. What will this house sell for? How heavy will this baby be at birth?
Classification, when the outcome is categorical. Will this patient’s cancer come back, yes or no?

Today we’ll fit a linear regression. On Wednesday we’ll fit linear and logistic regressions on medical data.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Models need tidy data
A model formula like price ~ sqft expects the data to have one row per observation (each house sale) and one column per variable (the price and the size), which is what tidy data gives us.

title: From tidy data to models
section: Linear regression: the line of best fit
text:
Linear regression: the line of best fit
\[
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The “best” line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances between the line and the data points.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Fit it with tidymodels

house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)

title: From tidy data to models
text:
More than one predictor
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_m X_m
\]
To use more predictors, we add them to the formula.

recipe(price ~ sqft + beds + baths, data = Sacramento)

Now each slope is how much the outcome changes for one predictor, when the other predictors stay the same.

title: Cleaning and tidying medical data
text:
Before we can model data, it has to be “tidy” and “clean”: one row per observation, one column per variable, and values coded the way we’ll analyze them. In class, we’ll reshape data into a tidy shape, then recode numbers into categories we can read. For more practice, see Extra practice: cleaning and tidying.
library(tidyverse)
library(medicaldata)

title: Cleaning and tidying medical data
section: Exercise 1: Gum health over the trial’s visits
text:
Exercise 1: Gum health over the trial’s visits
opt (from medicaldata) is the Obstetrics and Periodontal Therapy trial, which randomized pregnant women with periodontal disease to periodontal treatment (T) or control (C) (Michalowicz et al., 2006). Their gums were examined at baseline (BL), visit 3 (V3), and visit 5 (V5). We’ll look at two of the measures:

GE, the gingival index, where higher means more inflamed gums
PD.avg, the average pocket depth in millimetres

Every dataset in medicaldata is a base R data frame, not a tibble, so printing one prints every row. We’ll use head() to print just the first 6.

gums <- opt |>
  select(PID, Group, BL.GE, BL.PD.avg, V3.GE, V3.PD.avg, V5.GE, V5.PD.avg)
head(gums)

     PID Group BL.GE BL.PD.avg V3.GE V3.PD.avg V5.GE V5.PD.avg
1 100034     C 1.429     2.696 1.637     3.000 2.077     2.929
2 100042     C 1.298     2.685    NA        NA    NA        NA
3 100067     T 1.784     2.821    NA        NA    NA        NA
4 100083     C 1.596     2.814 1.000     3.660 1.000     3.660
5 100091     C 1.173     2.768 1.762     2.744 1.845     2.786
6 100109     T 0.969     2.932    NA        NA    NA        NA








NoteYour turn



A header like V3.PD.avg packs two variables into one name: the visit (V3) and the measure (PD.avg). PD.avg has a dot of its own, so names_sep = "." would split it in the wrong place. The names_pattern below reads “the visit, a dot, then the rest”.

Pivot the six measure columns into visit, measure, and value, dropping missing values.
Pivot measure back out, so GE and PD.avg are their own columns. Call the result gums_tidy.
Calculate the mean pocket depth and gingival index for each group at each visit. What happened to the treatment group’s gums?
Plot the mean pocket depth at each visit, coloured by group.


gums_tidy <- gums |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ____,
    names_to = c(____, ____),
    names_pattern = "(BL|V3|V5)\\.(.*)",
    values_to = "value",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = ____, values_from = ____)

gums_summary <- gums_tidy |>
  group_by(____, ____) |>
  summarize(
    avg_pd = mean(PD.avg, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_ge = mean(GE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ggplot(gums_summary, aes(x = visit, y = ____, colour = ____, group = ____)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Back to Sacramento
On Monday we fit price ~ sqft on the Sacramento house sales. Let’s add type, a categorical variable, so we can see how to read both kinds of variables.

Sacramento |>
  count(type)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  type             n
  <fct>        <int>
1 Condo           53
2 Multi_Family    13
3 Residential    866

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Dummy variables

A regression needs numbers, so R turns a categorical variable (a factor) into dummy variables, also called indicator variables
Each dummy variable is a 0/1 column for one level, and there’s one for every level except the first
The level without a column is the reference level, and every other level gets compared with it

title: Interpreting a linear regression
section: Two names for the same idea
text:
Two names for the same idea

Statistics calls this dummy variable encoding
Computer science and machine learning call it one-hot encoding
Both turn each level of a categorical variable into a 0/1 column
One-hot encoding usually keeps a column for every level, while a regression with an intercept drops one, the reference level (R does this for us)

type as dummy variables

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Interpreting a continuous variable

For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect [outcome] to increase (or decrease) by [estimate] [units], all else remaining the same.

For sqft:

For every 1 square foot increase in size, we expect the sale price to increase by $139, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $131 to $146).


“All else remaining the same” means the other variables in the model, so here, a house of the same type

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Interpreting a categorical variable

We expect [outcome] for [level] to be [estimate] [units] higher (or lower) than for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For typeMulti_Family:

We expect multi-family homes to sell for $66,224 less than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $14,762 to $117,686 less).


Here “all else” is the size: a multi-family home and a condo with the same square footage
The comparison is always with the reference level, Condo

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
When the interval includes 0
For typeResidential:

We expect residential homes to sell for $8,253 more than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: -$15,594 to $32,100).


The interval includes 0, so the data don’t show a clear difference between residential homes and condos of the same size
We still report the estimate and its interval, and say that it’s unclear

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
The intercept

The intercept is the expected outcome when every continuous variable is 0 and every categorical variable is at its reference level
Here that’s a condo with 0 square feet, which doesn’t exist, so we don’t interpret it

title: Observational units
text:
The original third rule
The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

title: Observational units
section: Problem 5: one unit in many tables
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables
The opposite problem is one kind of observation split across many files, such as one file per year or one per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them with bind_rows() or give read_csv() all the file names at once.

title: Observational units
text:
How hospitals store data
Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule, with one table per kind of observational unit, linked by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake but realistic patient records stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients in CSV, HL7 FHIR, and C-CDA formats.

title: Observational units
text:
Beyond CSVs: health data standards
In practice, health data is usually stored and shared using data standards, not as a folder of CSV files.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, which sends a patient, an encounter, or an observation as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on many hospitals’ databases

All of these follow the third rule, with one table (or resource) per kind of observational unit, linked by IDs.

Synthea synthetic patient records: https://synthetichealth.github.io/synthea/
Standards: HL7, FHIR, OHDSI and its OMOP Common Data Model.

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
A sore throat after surgery
licorice_gargle (from medicaldata) is a trial of 235 adults having thoracic surgery with a large breathing tube. Before the tube went in, they were randomized to gargle licorice or sugar water. Our outcome is any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Recode the variables

sore <- licorice_gargle |>
  mutate(
    sore_throat = factor(pacu30min_throatPain > 0,
                         levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("no", "yes")),
    treatment = factor(treat, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("sugar", "licorice")),
    smoking = factor(preOp_smoking, levels = c(3, 2, 1),
                     labels = c("never", "past",
                                "current"))
  ) |>
  select(sore_throat, treatment,
         bmi = preOp_calcBMI, smoking) |>
  drop_na()

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Which level are we modelling?

logistic_reg() models the odds of the outcome’s second level
sore_throat has the levels no, then yes, so every result is about the odds of a sore throat
The predictors are a mix of both kinds:

treatment: 2 levels, so 1 dummy variable (reference sugar)
bmi: continuous, in kg/m²
smoking: 3 levels, so 2 dummy variables (reference never)



count(sore, sore_throat)

  sore_throat   n
1          no 169
2         yes  64

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Fit the model

sore_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
      data = sore)

tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         0.0240    0.979     0.0245 0.980      -1.91     1.95  
2 treatmentlicorice  -0.956     0.316    -3.02   0.00252    -1.59    -0.346 
3 bmi                -0.0517    0.0385   -1.34   0.179      -0.129    0.0229
4 smokingpast         1.48      0.428     3.45   0.000551    0.664    2.35  
5 smokingcurrent      0.635     0.410     1.55   0.121      -0.152    1.46  



These estimates are on the log-odds scale, \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)\), which is hard to read

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Exponentiate to get odds ratios

sore_or <- sore_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
sore_or

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 



exponentiate = TRUE turns each estimate and its interval into an odds ratio (std.error, statistic, and p.value stay on the log-odds scale)
An odds ratio of 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower odds, and above 1 means higher odds

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Interpreting a continuous variable

For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio], all else remaining the same.

For bmi:

For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI, we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by 0.95, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.88 to 1.02).


Multiplied by 0.95 is the same as 5% lower odds
The interval includes 1, so the data don’t show a clear effect of BMI

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Interpreting a categorical variable

We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level] to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For treatmentlicorice:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice to be 0.38 times the odds for patients who gargled sugar water, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.71).


That’s 62% lower odds, and the interval doesn’t include 1

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
section: A categorical variable with more levels
text:
A categorical variable with more levels
Each dummy variable compares one level with the reference, never. For smokingpast:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for past smokers to be 4.38 times the odds for people who never smoked, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 1.94 to 10.48).


smokingcurrent compares current smokers with people who never smoked, not with past smokers
Its interval (0.86 to 4.33) includes 1, so that comparison isn’t clear

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Odds, not probability

An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities
Say “0.38 times the odds”, not “0.38 times as likely” or “62% less likely”
The two are close only when the outcome is rare, and here 27% of patients had a sore throat

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
section: The same model in base R
text:
The same model in base R
Base R’s glm() fits the same model with less code:

glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
    family = binomial, data = sore) |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 



family = binomial is what makes glm() a logistic regression
The same odds ratios and intervals as logistic_reg()
We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps

t.test(Birthweight ~ Group, data = opt_clean, var.equal = TRUE)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  Birthweight by Group
t = 0.50991, df = 791, p-value = 0.6103
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group control and group treatment is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -59.88793 101.91954

title: The class notes prompt
text:
This is all AI/Claude generated

We are building one prompt together that turns a class transcript into notes. You propose changes, we merge them, and all of the course’s notes get regenerated from the result — so an improvement you make after the lab also improves the notes for the lecture.



File
What it is




prompt-notes.md
The prompt. Every word of it is sent to the model, followed by a session’s transcript and slides. This is the file we edit together.


prompt-notes-<name>.md
Optional variants, for trying an idea next to the main prompt (see below).


README-prompt.md
This file: how it all works, and how to change it.


Makefile
Shortcuts for running the generator (make notes and the others below).





Each class session has a folder under sessions/, named by date — with a suffix such as -lecture or -lab when there were two classes that day:







File
What it is




plaud.md
share link to the recording


transcript-plaud.md
the transcript: machine-generated, lightly cleaned up by Plaud ← input


materials.md
the session’s slides from the course website: their text, the R code, and the output it printed, each heading linked to its slide ← input


notes-plaud.md
Plaud’s own AI notes — the baseline to beat


notes-class-main--<model>.md
what prompt-notes.md produced, and which model wrote it ← output



Reading notes-plaud.md and notes-class-main--<model>.md side by side is the point. Plaud’s notes come from a generic summariser that has never heard of this course. Ours know what the course is about, turn “see you Wednesday” into a real date, and keep the questions people asked.
The slides make a big difference. Speech is a bad way to record code: a microphone hears “percent greater percent” where the slide says %>%, and the arguments disappear. The instructor live-codes from the slides, so the prompt treats them as the authority on what was typed and what it printed, and links each piece of code back to its slide.
Notes come from more than one model: Claude (--claude-opus-…) and open-weights Qwen models run on the instructor’s own hardware (--qwen…), so you can compare them too.



Ordinary Git and GitHub practice. From a terminal:

Terminal
git switch -c prompt/your-change-here      # new branch
$EDITOR prompt-notes.md                    # make your edit
git add prompt-notes.md
git commit -m "Ask for a glossary of new functions"
git push -u origin prompt/your-change-here

Or on GitHub itself: open prompt-notes.md, click the pencil icon, make your edit, and choose Create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request.
In the pull request, say what problem the change fixes. The convincing version is a before/after on one session (see below), quoting the part that got better. A good change fixes something you can point at — a section that comes out thin, a date the notes got wrong, a kind of content the notes keep dropping. “Make it better” is not something we can evaluate.
To try a bigger idea next to the main prompt instead of in place of it, copy it to prompt-notes-<name>.md (say prompt-notes-glossary.md). Its notes come out as notes-class-glossary--<model>.md, beside the main ones, so the two can be compared.



The generator is class_notes.py, in the class-notes/scripts/ folder of the public chendaniely/skills repository. It needs Python 3 and, for Claude models, the Claude Code CLI, logged in once (claude, then /login). It runs on your Claude subscription: no API key is needed.

Terminal
git clone https://github.com/chendaniely/skills ~/git/skills      # once
cn=~/git/skills/class-notes/scripts/class_notes.py

python3 $cn generate --dry-run                                     # what would run
python3 $cn generate --only sessions/2026-11-02 --prompt glossary
python3 $cn generate --only sessions/2026-11-02 --force --model sonnet
python3 $cn payload --only sessions/2026-11-02 > message.txt

payload prints the exact message the model receives — the prompt, the transcript and the slides — so you can take a session to any other tool or model and do your own thing with it. No Claude subscription? Paste that message into GitHub Copilot Chat in your Codespace, or another assistant. The Makefile wraps the common runs (make notes, make notes-force); point it at your copy with CLASS_NOTES=~/git/skills/class-notes/scripts/class_notes.py.



There is one prompt file, not v1.md, v2.md, v3.md: git log -p prompt-notes.md shows every revision with its diff. Every generated notes file ends with a footer that records where it came from:
---

- prompt: prompt-notes.md @ a1b2c3d
- prompt-hash: 3f9c0e2b7a41
- model: claude-opus-5-5 (requested: opus)
- backend: claude
- inputs: transcript-plaud.md, materials.md
- generated: 2026-11-04
opus is an alias meaning “the latest Opus”, and what it points at changes over time; claude-opus-5-5 is the model that actually ran, which is why it is also in the filename. When the alias moves to a newer model, regenerated notes land in a new file next to the old one, so models can be compared too. inputs says whether the notes had the slides or only the transcript. prompt-hash is a fingerprint of the prompt’s words, so a commit that doesn’t change them (a rename, a revert) never makes old notes look out of date. A prompt shown as @ uncommitted was run before that version of it was committed; the prompt-hash still pins down its exact words.



These transcripts include your voices, and this repository is public on GitHub, so anyone can read them, and anyone with a session’s plaud.md link can play its recording. Students appear in the transcript as Speaker 1, Speaker 2, and so on. The prompt instructs the model to keep it that way and never to attach a name to a question. If you change the prompt, keep that rule.
