title: Observational Units, Linear Regression, and Logistic Regression
text:
This second session began with setup. Students opened the course repository in a GitHub Codespace, learned how to fork it, and learned how to render a Quarto document to HTML and PDF. The instructor also showed the “AI class notes” section of the course website, where each lecture’s transcript and AI-generated summaries are posted. He introduced Positron, an IDE from the RStudio team that is built on VS Code, as an alternative to RStudio. Several Codespaces problems, including the instructor’s own, came up and were worked through.
The content picked up the third rule of the original tidy data paper: each type of observational unit forms a table. Using the tidy Billboard data from Lecture 1, the instructor split the song information and the weekly rankings into two tables linked by an id column, then joined them back together. He compared this to how hospitals store data, with a patients table keyed by a medical record number and an encounters table that refers to it. He pointed to Synthea for synthetic hospital data and to HL7, FHIR, and the OMOP Common Data Model as real-world standards.
Most of the session covered the two baseline models: linear regression for a numeric outcome and logistic regression for a binary outcome. The class fit price ~ sqft + type on the Sacramento house sales with linear_reg(). They learned how a categorical predictor becomes dummy variables with a reference level, and practised turning coefficients from tidy() into fill-in-the-blank interpretation sentences. They then fit a logistic regression on the licorice_gargle trial from medicaldata. They saw that its raw estimates are log odds, used tidy(exponentiate = TRUE) to convert them to odds ratios, and interpreted those ratios against the reference levels. The instructor stressed that odds are not probabilities.
After the break, the instructor walked through the homework and demonstrated agentic coding on the Ebola question. He warned strongly about what coding agents can see and do. They print your data and files back to the model provider, they can read password files, and they can delete things. For that reason, patient data must never go through a personal AI subscription. The session ended with practical advice on saving work in a Codespace and an explanation of why a date parsed with mdy() prints in year-month-day order.

title: Observational Units, Linear Regression, and Logistic Regression
text:
GitHub Codespace: a cloud copy of the course repository, already set up with R, Quarto, the Quarto extension, and the packages. You open it from the green Code button, then the Codespaces tab, then “Create codespace on main”. The first start takes around ten minutes, and later starts are faster.

Keep your Codespace tab open. An idle Codespace goes to sleep and shuts down after about 20 minutes of inactivity, and you then have to wait for it to start again.
Each Codespace gets a random name, such as “organic barnacle” or “fuzzy fiesta”. You only need one.
A free account limits how many Codespaces you can have at once. If you see a “maximum codespaces reached” error, go to github.com/codespaces and delete the extra ones.

Saving work in a Codespace (warning): saving a file saves it inside that Codespace instance, not back to Git.

Closing the tab does not delete the Codespace. It is like turning off a laptop: as long as you return to the same named Codespace, your work is still there.
Deleting the Codespace deletes your work. That is like throwing the laptop away.
The easiest way to keep your homework is to copy the whole homework.qmd (Ctrl+A, Ctrl+C) and paste it into a file on your own computer. If you know Git, you can add, commit, and push to your fork from VS Code’s Git panel, but that is out of scope for this course.

Fork: makes a copy of the repository under your own GitHub account, so you keep it even if the original is removed. When the instructor makes changes, a Sync fork button pulls his updates into your copy. You do not need a fork for class.
Download ZIP: if Git makes no sense to you, use the green Code button and choose Download ZIP. The ZIP contains the homework and all the data. There is no Git requirement in this course.
Local setup: if you work on your own computer, you need R, RStudio (or Positron), and Quarto. Quarto is a separate install from the Quarto website: go to the current release and pick your operating system. The course site’s “local setup” page has a block of package installs (tidyverse, tidymodels, medicaldata, and a few others) to copy into your R console.
Positron: a newer IDE from the people who make RStudio. It is essentially VS Code, the editor you see in a Codespace, with RStudio features added, such as a variable viewer and a plot viewer. It works with both R and Python, and it comes with Quarto support built in.

VS Code and Codespaces have no environment or variable viewer. To see an object there, you print it from a code chunk.

Rendering a Quarto document: render the homework to both HTML and PDF, using the “render all formats” option.

In Positron there is a Preview button at the top.
In a Codespace or VS Code, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac) and run the Quarto render command. If you open the palette by clicking instead, type > first so it searches commands.
In plain VS Code (not in a Codespace), install the Quarto extension from the Extensions panel on the left.
In RStudio, click the Render button.
Rendering runs all the code, captures the output, and writes the HTML and PDF next to the .qmd. You submit all three files.

Quarto vs R Markdown: Quarto is the successor to R Markdown. R Markdown is still supported but will not get new features.

The syntax is very similar: code cells use three backticks and curly braces.
In R Markdown, websites, blogs, and documents each need a separate package. Quarto bundles all of them, is a little faster, and works better with languages other than R.
The course slides themselves are made with Quarto.

AI class notes: the course site has a section with each lecture’s transcript, an AI summary from Anthropic’s model, and summaries from local models for comparison, along with the prompt that was used. One suggested way to use them is to skim the main headings and check whether you understand each concept.





The original third rule: the 2014 Tidy Data paper’s third rule is “each type of observational unit forms a table”. The newer, commonly taught version says each cell holds one value.

An observational unit is the kind of thing you observe, such as a song, a patient, or a hospital visit.

Duplication in the tidy Billboard data: in billboard_tidy, the song information (year, artist, track, time) repeats on every row for every week the song charted, up to dozens of times per song. This causes two problems:

It is inefficient storage.
It makes edits risky. Fixing one spelling means changing it on every repeated row, and a blanket rename could hit two different artists’ songs that share a title.

The analysis table vs the storage tables: the long table with everything repeated is what you need for analysis, for example to group by artist or track. For storage, you split it into a song table (one row per song, with a new id) and a rank table (id, week, date, rank). When an analysis needs both, you join them back on id.
The hospital parallel: a patients table holds each patient’s demographics once, keyed by a medical record number (MRN), which usually just increments by one for each new patient. An encounters table holds visits with only the MRN, for example a radiology X-ray. If a birthday is corrected in patients, every encounter sees the correction.

To answer something like “the average age of people coming into radiology for an X-ray”, you join patients and encounters.
MRNs are private: an MRN lets someone look up a person’s demographics and everything else that happened to them.

Why this matters: the analysis-ready datasets you are given were usually assembled by someone else. When you build your own, you need to know where the pieces come from. If you write data back to a database, you write it in the split form.
Synthea: synthetic but realistic hospital records stored this way, available as CSV and also in HL7 FHIR and C-CDA formats. It comes in sizes from 100 patients up to very large populations. It is a safe way to practise.

The instructor’s dissertation materials include a walkthrough using Synthea’s encounters and patients data. It finds patients admitted with a myocardial infarction and checks whether they return to the emergency department within 30 days.

Health data standards: HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data. FHIR is HL7’s newer standard.
OMOP Common Data Model (from the OHDSI community): a shared database layout. If hospitals follow it, you can send your code rather than the protected patient data, and each site runs the same analysis on its own data. This is how multi-site and international studies work.

OMOP includes vocabulary mappings between coding systems, such as SNOMED, ICD-9, ICD-10, and national codes.






Baseline models: linear and logistic regression are the first models to try. They are fast, and they give simple sentences that are easy to interpret.

“Best model” in machine learning is always relative to something, so these models serve as the baseline you compare other models against.

Interpretability matters in health: in health care, and in regulated areas like finance, you may have to explain why a treatment or policy changes. “The computer made a guess” is not an acceptable rationale when a patient’s care is at stake.
The single most important question: what are you trying to measure or predict, and can you point to that column?

If you cannot point to it, your data is not tidy yet and needs cleaning.

The outcome’s type decides the model:

A numeric outcome (for example price, or a blood value like albumin) calls for linear regression.
A binary categorical outcome calls for logistic regression.
Predictors can be continuous or categorical in either model. Only the left side of the ~ decides which model you use.

Treating ordered stages as numbers: some studies treat disease stages as numbers even though they are not really numbers. When you see that, ask why they did it.
Any categorical outcome can be made binary: for example “cancer yes or no”, “stage 1 to 2 vs stage 3 to 4”, or “is this house a condo, yes or no?”.
Class imbalance (common pitfall): always check the frequency counts during exploratory data analysis.

In Sacramento, the type counts are very uneven: 53 condos, 13 multi-family homes, and 866 residential homes.
If 99 of 100 emails are not spam, a model that never flags spam is 99% accurate and completely useless at its one job.
The same problem affects rare diseases.
In licorice_gargle, 169 patients had no sore throat and 64 did. A model that always says “no” would be right about three quarters of the time.
Better metrics for this are covered in a machine learning course, not here.






Dummy variables (also called indicator variables): a regression needs numbers, so R turns a factor with n levels into n − 1 0/1 columns.

The level without its own column is the reference level, and every other level is compared with it.
Tidymodels and R do this for you automatically.

One-hot encoding: the computer science and machine learning name for the same idea. One-hot encoding usually keeps a column for every level. A regression with an intercept drops one level, the reference.
Encoding type: type has 3 levels, so it becomes typeMulti_Family and typeResidential. A condo is 0 in both columns, which is how its value can be inferred without a column of its own.
How R picks the reference level: R uses the first level of the factor. You can change it, and doing so is part of the data cleaning you do for modelling.

When a categorical variable has many levels, check which one is missing from the output. That missing level is your reference, and it is easy to overlook.

Data cleaning never ends: you clean once for exploratory data analysis and again for modelling. The model itself is only about two lines of code.





Fitting: linear_reg() |> fit(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento). The outcome goes to the left of the ~ and the predictors go to the right.
tidy(): turns a fitted model into a data frame of coefficients, called the coefficient table. You can plot it or save it as a CSV.

The estimate column is what you use to build interpretation sentences.
p-values, AIC/BIC, and degrees of freedom matter in statistics and causal inference courses, which are beyond this class.

Interpreting a continuous variable: “For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect [outcome] to increase (or decrease) by [estimate] [units], all else remaining the same.”

Example: “For every 1 square foot increase in size, we expect the sale price to increase by $139, all else remaining the same.”
Know your units: if a variable has been standardized (z-scored), “one unit” means one standard deviation, not one unit of the original measurement.
All else remaining the same: you interpret one number at a time, holding the other predictors fixed. Here, that means a house of the same type.

Interpreting a categorical variable: “We expect [outcome] for [level] to be [estimate] [units] higher (or lower) than for [reference level], all else remaining the same.” The “one unit increase” is the move from the reference level (0) to this level (1).

Example for typeMulti_Family: “We expect multi-family homes to sell for $66,224 less than condos, all else remaining the same.”
Example for typeResidential: “We expect residential homes to sell for $8,253 more than condos of the same square footage.”
Each dummy variable gets its own coefficient and its own sentence. You do not interpret type as a whole.

Choosing the reference level: the math does not care which level is the reference, but the human-readable sentence does.

For disease stages, use stage 1 (or no disease) as the reference, not a middle stage.
Changing the reference changes the estimates and possibly their signs.

The intercept: the expected outcome when every continuous variable is 0 and every categorical variable is at its reference level. Here, that is a 0-square-foot condo, which does not exist, so we don’t interpret it.

You still need the intercept to compute predictions.
Do not read it as “the cost of the land”. That would need a separate model.

Interpreting vs predicting: these are two different uses of the same model.

To interpret, you read one coefficient at a time.
To predict, you need all of the inputs for the case at hand, then multiply each coefficient by its value, add them up, and add the intercept. For example, a 1,000 square foot residential home gets 1,000 × 139 = $139,000 from sqft, plus $8,253 for being residential, plus the intercept.

The formula: with one predictor, the model is the statistics version of y = mx + b: the outcome equals the intercept plus a coefficient times the predictor. With more predictors, each one adds its own β·x term, and a categorical predictor adds one term per dummy variable. The β values are the estimates in the coefficient table.
Adding covariates: more covariates do not make interpretation harder. The table gets longer, and the numbers change because each estimate now accounts for the other variables.

Which variables belong in the model is a research and experimental design question, involving confounders and colliders from epidemiology. It is not a coding question.

Base R equivalent: lm(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento) piped into tidy() gives the same table. The class uses tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps.





The data: licorice_gargle (from medicaldata) is a randomized trial of 235 adults having thoracic surgery. Before intubation, patients gargled licorice or sugar water. The outcome is any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.
Recoding before modelling:

sore_throat becomes a factor with levels no then yes.
treatment comes from treat: 0 = sugar (the reference), 1 = licorice.
smoking comes from preOp_smoking: 3 = never (the reference), 2 = past, 1 = current.
bmi comes from preOp_calcBMI and is continuous, in kg/m².
Raw numeric codes like these mean you have to look up the codebook to know what each number stands for.

Which level is modelled: logistic_reg() models the odds of the outcome’s second level. Since the levels of sore_throat are no then yes, every result is about the odds of a sore throat.
Fitting: same as linear regression, swapping linear_reg() for logistic_reg(). The formula, fit(), and tidy() are unchanged.

The running joke is that machine learning is not that hard; it’s all the other work around it.

Why a transformation is needed: a straight line would predict values below 0 and above 1, and a prediction of 0.5 makes no sense for a category. Logistic regression applies the log-odds transformation, log(p / (1 − p)), to bound the line between 0 and 1.
Generalized linear models (GLMs): logistic regression belongs to the GLM family, as do Poisson models. They all transform a straight line to fit the data, and you undo the transformation to write an interpretable sentence.
Raw estimates are log odds: the sentence structure still works (“For every 1 unit increase in BMI, we expect the log odds to decrease by 0.0517”), but log odds mean nothing to a human reader.
Odds ratios: exponentiating undoes the log. Use tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE), or exponentiate the column yourself with mutate().

An odds ratio of 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower odds, and above 1 means higher odds.
std.error, statistic, and p.value stay on the log-odds scale.
Odds ratios are everywhere in epidemiology, with its 2×2 tables, because so many outcomes there are binary.

Interpreting a continuous variable: “For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio], all else remaining the same.”

Example: “For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI, we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by 0.95, all else remaining the same.”

Interpreting a categorical variable: “We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level] to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level], all else remaining the same.”

Example: licorice vs sugar water gives 0.38 times the odds.
With more levels, each dummy variable compares one level with the reference. Past smokers have 4.38 times the odds of people who never smoked. smokingcurrent compares current smokers with never-smokers, not with past smokers.

Odds, not probability (common mistake): odds are p / (1 − p), which is not the same as probability.

Thinking “probability” in your head may help you make sense of the sentence, but never write it down that way.
Say “0.38 times the odds”, not “0.38 times as likely”.

Describing the reference group: you don’t interpret the reference group on its own. It is the baseline everything else is compared with. If you care about a particular group, make a different level the reference, for example “compared with frequent smokers, never-smokers’ odds are…”.
Base R equivalent: glm(..., family = binomial) piped into tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) gives the same table. family = binomial is what makes glm() a logistic regression.





Work in small steps: when learning, have the agent write only a few lines at a time.

“Go clean this data set” gives you a hundred lines you can’t follow. Even “tidy the Ebola data” is four steps.
Ask for the next step, run it, and look at the output.

How an agent sees your data: an agent does not see R’s environment the way RStudio does. To look at your data, it writes code that prints the files and data, and that output goes to the model provider, such as Anthropic.

Never use your own AI subscription on hospital or patient data. Identifiable data like patient names and MRNs leak exactly this way, and this is where data breaches happen.
Use only an agent your hospital has sanctioned, which normally means one with an agreement and a privately deployed model. Otherwise, practise on synthetic data such as Synthea.

Agents can read passwords and delete things: an agent lists the files on your computer. If you have a passwords file, it can read it, and it can write and run code that deletes data.

The approve or allow button in Copilot is the human review step, and it is essentially the only thing stopping the agent from doing something you didn’t expect.
A web chatbot like ChatGPT cannot read your files unless you paste them in. An agent can.

Agents make mistakes: in the live demo, the agent put the solution for the wrong problem at the line it was given. Free tiers, such as the Codespaces Copilot, use smaller models, so review even more carefully there.

You can steer the agent: “we learned this function in class, can you use it?”

Your job shifts to checking: agents make fewer typos, so you see less red error text. The harder question becomes whether the code did the right thing.

Run the code yourself and check that the output looks right.
Ask the agent to explain any part you don’t understand, such as a pivot_longer() step.
In health settings, code can put a patient’s life on the line. Using these tools does not remove your responsibility.

Models misread figures: in a study the instructor described, researchers flipped the horsepower vs miles-per-gallon trend in the mtcars data. The model still described the trend as negative, because that is what it expected.

Have your own sense of a figure before asking a model about it.
A better approach is to write your own rough caption and ask the model to improve it.

Prompting is about context: give the model the specific technical vocabulary from class. The homework is long precisely because it holds that context.





mdy(): names the format of the input string. The Ebola Date column is read as character text in month/day/year order, so you parse it with mdy(). Functions exist for the other orders too, such as ymd().
Why the date prints as year-month-day: after parsing, the column is a real date object, and dates print in the ISO 8601 standard order, year-month-day.

Once it is a date, date arithmetic works (one date minus another). Date arithmetic does not work on a character string, even one that looks like year-month-day; you would convert it with ymd() first.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)    # linear_reg(), logistic_reg(), tidy(); also loads Sacramento
library(medicaldata)   # licorice_gargle



billboard_tidy <- read_csv("data/billboard.csv") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",                          # "wk1" -> "1"
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE                         # drop weeks a song wasn't charting
  ) |>
  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |> # date of each chart week
  arrange(artist, track, week) |>
  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)
billboard_tidy
The song information repeats on every week’s row:
# A tibble: 5,307 × 7
    year artist  track                   time    week  rank date
 1  2000 2 Pac   Baby Don't Cry (Keep... 04:22      1    87 2000-02-26
 2  2000 2 Pac   Baby Don't Cry (Keep... 04:22      2    82 2000-03-04
 3  2000 2 Pac   Baby Don't Cry (Keep... 04:22      3    72 2000-03-11



song <- billboard_tidy |>
  distinct(artist, track, year, time) |>       # one row per unique song
  mutate(id = row_number(), .before = 1)       # new ID, like a hospital MRN
song

rank <- billboard_tidy |>
  left_join(song, by = c("artist", "track", "year", "time")) |>  # attach the id
  select(id, week, date, rank)                 # drop the repeated song info
rank
The result is 317 songs, each stored once, and 5,307 ranking rows that carry only the id:
# A tibble: 317 × 5
      id artist         track                    year time
 1     1 2 Pac          Baby Don't Cry (Keep...  2000 04:22
 2     2 2Ge+her        The Hardest Part Of ...  2000 03:15

# A tibble: 5,307 × 4
      id  week date        rank
 1     1     1 2000-02-26    87
 2     1     2 2000-03-04    82



rank |>
  left_join(song, by = "id")   # rebuilds the analysis table (5,307 × 8)



Sacramento |>
  count(type)
  type             n
1 Condo           53
2 Multi_Family    13
3 Residential    866
The counts are badly imbalanced. Condo comes first, so it becomes the reference level.



house_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento)   # outcome ~ predictors

house_tidy <- tidy(house_fit, conf.int = TRUE)  # coefficient table as a data frame
house_tidy
  term             estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
1 (Intercept)         6885.  12169.       0.566 5.72e-  1  -16996.    30766.
2 sqft                 139.      3.88    35.7   1.64e-176     131.      146.
3 typeMulti_Family  -66224.  26222.      -2.53  1.17e-  2 -117686.   -14762.
4 typeResidential     8253.  12151.       0.679 4.97e-  1  -15594.    32100.
The table has one row per dummy variable and no row for Condo, the reference. The 139, −66,224, and 8,253 estimates are the numbers interpreted in Knowledge Points 5.



lm(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento) |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE)                         # identical table



sore <- licorice_gargle |>
  mutate(
    sore_throat = factor(pacu30min_throatPain > 0,          # any pain at 30 min
                         levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("no", "yes")),          # "yes" is 2nd level, so it's modelled
    treatment = factor(treat, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("sugar", "licorice")),    # sugar = reference
    smoking = factor(preOp_smoking, levels = c(3, 2, 1),    # codebook: 3 = never
                     labels = c("never", "past",
                                "current"))                 # never = reference
  ) |>
  select(sore_throat, treatment,
         bmi = preOp_calcBMI, smoking) |>                   # rename while selecting
  drop_na()



count(sore, sore_throat)
  sore_throat   n
1          no 169
2         yes  64



sore_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
      data = sore)

tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE)   # estimates are log odds
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
2 treatmentlicorice  -0.956     0.316    -3.02   0.00252    -1.59    -0.346
3 bmi                -0.0517    0.0385   -1.34   0.179      -0.129    0.0229
4 smokingpast         1.48      0.428     3.45   0.000551    0.664    2.35



sore_or <- sore_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)   # estimate and CI become odds ratios
sore_or
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33
These give “0.38 times the odds” for licorice vs sugar, “multiplied by 0.95” per kg/m² of BMI, and “4.38 times the odds” for past vs never smokers.



glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
    family = binomial, data = sore) |>          # family = binomial makes it logistic
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

title: Observational Units, Linear Regression, and Logistic Regression
text:
Q: A student had forked the repository and opened a Codespace from their fork. Is that right? A: Either works for class. Open the Codespace from your fork only if you want to work in your own copy.
Q: Do we have to download the Quarto extension first? A: Not in a Codespace, where it is already installed, and not in Positron, which comes with it. In plain VS Code, search “Quarto” in the Extensions panel and click Install. In RStudio, with Quarto installed, use the Render button.
Q: When I press the Quarto render button it says there was an error, and then my Codespace stops. Is there a maximum number of running Codespaces? A: Yes. A free account can only have a limited number. Go to github.com/codespaces and delete the extra ones, and that frees up space.
Q: Is the one we’re using today the one called “organic barnacle”? A: Codespace names are random; his was “fuzzy fiesta”. The repository it comes from is shown at the top. You should only have one, so delete the others.
Q: My only Codespace now says “stopping” instead of “setting up”. A: Wait for it to restart.
Q: How do you install Quarto? A: It is already in the Codespace. On your own computer, go to the Quarto website, choose the current release for your operating system, and install it like a normal program. RStudio may bundle Quarto, but installing it separately is cleaner.
Q: Why Quarto instead of R Markdown? A: Quarto is the successor to R Markdown. R Markdown is still supported but won’t get new features. The syntax is nearly identical. Quarto bundles documents, websites, and slides in one tool, is faster, and handles languages other than R better. These slides come straight out of Quarto.
Q: Does it matter what your reference value is? A: Not to the math. It matters for the sentence you write. With disease stages, compare against stage 1 or no disease, not a middle stage, or the result is hard for a person to understand.
Q: Does it get more complicated to interpret if you have more covariates? A: No. You still interpret one number at a time, assuming everything else stays the same. The numbers themselves change as you add variables, because each estimate accounts for the others. Which variables to include, such as confounders and colliders, is an experimental design question.
Q: If you add more variables, such as the number of bedrooms and bathrooms, can you interpret each one on its own? A: Yes. The table just gets longer, with a separate estimate for each variable.
Q: If you add more variables, how do you get the price? A: Decide whether you are interpreting a variable or predicting the outcome. To predict, you need all of the inputs for that house. Multiply each by its coefficient (1,000 square feet × 139 gives $139,000), add $8,253 if it is residential, add the intercept, and sum everything.
Q: Can you make a sentence about the reference value, for example the odds for someone who doesn’t smoke? A: You don’t interpret the reference on its own; it is the baseline everything is compared to. If that group is what you care about, make a different level the reference, such as frequent smokers. Then you can say “compared with frequent smokers, never-smokers’ odds are…”.
Q: Do you have to fork in order to do the work? A: No. It only matters if you want to save your work in GitHub, and even then you can copy and paste the text out. You can also do the whole assignment in RStudio.
Q: Can we do the homework as R Markdown? A: Yes. Copy the .qmd, delete the Quarto format line, and save it as .Rmd, because RStudio will treat a .qmd as Quarto.
Q: If we do it in R on our own computer, how do we get the CSV? Is it part of a package? A: The data is in the repository’s folder. Click the green Code button and either clone or download the ZIP. That includes all the data and the website. The only file you need to edit is homework.qmd.
Q: The tidymodels code doesn’t run locally. Is there no interpreter? A: On your own computer you have to install the packages yourself, using the install code on the local setup page.
Q: Are we really writing code in the homework? A: Barely. Much of it is fill-in-the-blank, with very detailed instructions.
Q: I used mutate() with mdy(), but the dates still print as year-month-day. Why? A: mdy() describes the input. The original column is character text in month/day/year order. After mutate(), it is a real date object, and dates print in ISO 8601 order, year-month-day. Now date arithmetic works. A character column already in year-month-day order would still need ymd() before you could do date math.
Q: Is there an environment section in Codespaces where you can see the variables? A: No. Codespaces is built on VS Code, which has no variable viewer, so you print objects from a code chunk. Positron run locally has one.
Q: If I didn’t fork and I work in this Codespace, is my work saved? A: It is saved inside that Codespace, fork or not, but not back to Git. The easiest safeguard is to copy the whole homework file and save it on your computer.
Q: If I close my Codespaces tab, does that delete it? A: No. It shuts down after about 20 minutes of inactivity and you can start it again, and as long as you reopen the same named Codespace your work is there. Deleting it loses everything.
Q: What if I just get it done in one go? A: That’s totally valid. Doing it step by step or through the agent teaches you different things.

title: Observational Units, Linear Regression, and Logistic Regression
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables: the opposite problem, one kind of observation split across many files (one per year or site), stacked with bind_rows() or by giving read_csv() all the file names.
How hospitals store data: lists patients, encounters, and the conditions, medications, and observations tables, and links to Synthea’s downloads page.
When the interval includes 0: the residential estimate’s 95% CI (−$15,594 to $32,100) includes 0, so the data don’t show a clear difference from condos. You still report the estimate and say the difference is unclear.
Interpreting a continuous variable (linear): adds the 95% CI ($131 to $146) to the sqft sentence.
Interpreting a categorical variable (logistic): licorice gives 62% lower odds (95% CI 0.20 to 0.71), and the interval doesn’t include 1.
Interpreting a continuous variable (logistic): multiplying by 0.95 means 5% lower odds, and BMI’s interval (0.88 to 1.02) includes 1, so there is no clear effect.
A categorical variable with more levels: smokingcurrent’s interval (0.86 to 4.33) includes 1, so that comparison isn’t clear.
Odds, not probability: odds and probability are close only when the outcome is rare, and here 27% of patients had a sore throat.
Data and credits (linear regression): Sacramento comes from modeldata, and the interpretation follows Data Science: A First Introduction chapter 8 and Data Science for the Biomedical Sciences.
Data and credits (logistic regression): sources for licorice_gargle and the ds4biomed chapters on odds ratios with tidymodels.

title: Lecture 2: Observational units and interpreting regression models
text:
Date Time: 2026-11-04
Instructor: Daniel Chen


This session continued the biostatistics-with-tidyverse material by returning to the tidy-data paper’s idea of observational units. Using the Billboard example from Lecture 1, the instructor showed that a table that is tidy for analysis can still be inefficient for storage because song-level information such as year, artist, track, and time is repeated for every week a song appears on the chart. The remedy was to split the data into separate tables: one song table containing one row per unique song and an id column, and one rank table containing id, week, date, and rank. The two tables can later be recombined with left_join(). The instructor connected this pattern to hospital databases, where one table might contain patient demographics linked to patients by a medical record number, and another table might contain encounters, tests, or imaging results.
The second major part of the session was reading and interpreting regression models. The instructor introduced linear regression with the Sacramento house-sales data and price ~ sqft + type, and logistic regression with the licorice_gargle data from the medicaldata package. The emphasis was not on statistical theory but on practical interpretation: how categorical predictors become dummy variables, which level is the reference level, how to interpret continuous coefficients, how to interpret categorical coefficients as comparisons to the reference level, and how logistic-regression coefficients are reported on the log-odds scale before being exponentiated into odds ratios. The instructor also showed the equivalent base-R functions lm() and glm().
The session also included substantial practical material about working in GitHub Codespaces, RStudio, Positron, and Quarto, including how to render .qmd files to HTML and PDF, how Codespaces start, stop, sleep, and get deleted, and how to use agentic coding tools such as GitHub Copilot or Claude to help with the assignment. The instructor repeatedly stressed that coding agents can be useful but must be reviewed carefully, especially because they may write code that reads local files, prints data, or accidentally accesses sensitive information. The homework assignment involved tidying the Ebola dataset, making tables and figures, and fitting either a linear or logistic regression model.






Original third rule of tidy data:

Each variable forms a column.
Each observation forms a row.
Each type of observational unit forms a table.

Observational unit:

The kind of thing being observed.
Examples from class: a song, a patient, a hospital visit, a hospital encounter.

Tidy for analysis vs tidy for storage:

A single analysis table is often convenient for modeling and plotting.
But it may store the same information many times.
In the Billboard example, each song’s artist, track, year, and time was repeated for every week that song was on the chart.
For storage, it is better to separate repeated song information into its own table and link it by an ID.

Billboard split:

The analysis table contained one row per song-week ranking.
The storage-style design separated it into:

song: one row per unique song, with id, artist, track, year, and time.
rank: one row per ranking, with id, week, date, and rank.

distinct(artist, track, year, time) removed the repeated song rows.
mutate(id = row_number(), .before = 1) created a new integer id column and placed it at the front of the table.
left_join() was used to attach the song id back to the weekly ranking data.

Hospital database analogy:

Hospitals often store data in separate tables by observational unit.
Examples:

patients: one row per patient, with demographic information.
encounters: one row per visit, with the patient’s ID.
conditions, medications, and observations: one row per record, linked to patients and encounters by IDs.

To analyze the data, you join the tables you need into one tidy analysis table.

Why this matters for analysis:

If a patient’s birthday or demographic value is wrong, you only need to fix it in the patients table.
You do not need to fix it across every encounter, lab, imaging, or medication row.
Later analyses can join the cleaned patient table back to encounter or encounter-derived tables.

Synthea:

A project that creates synthetic, realistic hospital datasets.
Useful for practicing data structures without real patient data.
Available in smaller and larger sizes, including examples around 100 patients up to very large simulated hospitals.
Available in CSV format, which is friendly to introductory R work, as well as HL7 FHIR and C-CDA formats.

Health data standards:

HL7: family of standards used by hospital systems to exchange clinical data.
FHIR: HL7’s newer standard; sends a patient, encounter, or observation as a “resource” through web APIs.
OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community:

A shared database layout for observational health data.
Allows the same analysis code to run on many different hospital databases.
Supports multi-site analyses without emailing protected patient data between institutions.
Helps standardize coding systems, for example mapping different country-specific ICD codes into a common structure.


Instructor’s dissertation example:

The instructor mentioned a walkthrough for 30-day hospital readmissions.
It used Synthea-style data to find patients with a heart attack or myocardial infarction and check whether they returned to the emergency department within 30 days.
The example required combining patient-level data with encounter-level data.






GitHub Codespaces:

Students were directed to the course GitHub repository, click Code, then the Codespaces tab, and open the Codespace on main.
Opening a Codespace can take several minutes.
The Codespace environment is preconfigured for the course.

Forking the repository:

Forking makes a copy of the repository under the student’s GitHub account.
It is not required for the session.
It is mainly a backup option so the student has their own copy.
If the instructor later changes the original repository, a fork can be updated with Sync from Upstream.

If Git does not make sense:

Students could use the Download ZIP button to get the homework assignment and course files.
The important file for the assignment is the .qmd homework file.

Quarto:

Quarto is used to make reproducible reports by capturing code, output, and prose in one document.
It is the successor to R Markdown.
R Markdown is still supported, but new features are focused on Quarto.
Quarto bundles more functionality into one system and works better with multiple programming languages.
For the homework, students needed to render the document to HTML and PDF.
In RStudio or Positron, a render or preview button can be used.
In VS Code or Codespaces, the Quarto extension may be needed; in Positron it comes with the tool.
In Codespaces, if the button is not visible, open the Command Palette with Control+Shift+P / Command+Shift+P / Apple+Shift+P, or click the button that starts with >.
When using the Command Palette this way, type > first so it knows it is in command mode.
The render workflow should produce the Quarto file plus rendered HTML and PDF files.

Positron:

An IDE made by the same people behind RStudio.
It is essentially VS Code with many RStudio-like data-science features added.
It has a variable viewer and plot viewer on the right side.
It is not the same as the Codespace environment.
It can be useful for local work, especially if you also use Python and R.

Saving work in Codespaces:

Work is stored inside the Codespace instance.
Closing the browser tab does not delete the Codespace.
The Codespace can go to sleep or shut down after inactivity, but it can be restarted.
Deleting a Codespace removes its contents.
If you have not committed work to Git, deleting the Codespace can lose the work.
A simple safety measure is to copy and paste the .qmd file to your own computer.
If you know Git, you can also add, commit, and push changes to your fork.

Maximum Codespaces error:

Free GitHub accounts have a limit on how many Codespaces can be open.
If a new Codespace fails to start, go to github.com/codespaces and delete unused Codespaces.
Deleting an old, unused Codespace frees up a slot.
Do not delete the active Codespace containing your current work.






First question: what is the outcome?

The outcome is the thing you are trying to measure or predict.
It must be a column you can point to in the data.
If it is not a column, the data are not tidy enough for that model.

Continuous outcome:

Use linear regression.
Example: house price, blood values such as albumin, or other numeric quantities.
Linear regression estimates an expected value on the outcome’s original scale.

Categorical outcome:

Use logistic regression when the outcome is binary or can be collapsed into a binary question.
Example: sore throat yes / no.
A multi-level categorical variable can sometimes be collapsed into a binary one, for example “has cancer: yes/no” or “stage 1–2 vs stage 3–4.”

Predictors can be continuous or categorical:

The predictor variables do not determine whether you use linear or logistic regression.
The outcome variable determines the model family.
Predictors may be continuous, such as sqft or bmi, or categorical, such as type or treatment.

Why start with linear and logistic regression:

They are simple, fast, and interpretable.
They are good baseline models.
In healthcare and financial markets, interpretability can matter because you may need to explain why a treatment, policy, or decision changed.
More complex machine-learning models can be compared against these simpler baselines.

Class imbalance:

If one outcome category is much more common than another, a model can achieve high accuracy by always predicting the majority class.
Example: if almost no one gets a rare disease, a model that always says “no disease” can still have very high accuracy but may be useless for detecting the rare cases.
This matters for rare diseases, spam filters, and other imbalanced outcomes.
The class did not go deep into imbalance solutions; that is more advanced machine-learning or evaluation content.






Data used in class:

Sacramento house-sales data.
Outcome: price.
Predictors: sqft and type.

type as a categorical variable:

The observed levels were:

Condo
Multi_Family
Residential

Counts were imbalanced:

Condo: 53
Multi_Family: 13
Residential: 866


Dummy variables:

A regression needs numeric input, so R converts a categorical variable into dummy variables.
Statistics often calls this dummy variable encoding.
Computer science and machine learning often call the same idea one-hot encoding.
For a factor with n levels, a regression with an intercept uses n - 1 dummy variables.
The missing level is the reference level.
In the house example, Condo was the reference level because it was the first level.

House type dummy encoding:

typeMulti_Family:

1 if the house is Multi_Family.
0 otherwise.

typeResidential:

1 if the house is Residential.
0 otherwise.

Condo:

Represented by both dummy variables being 0.


Fitting the model:

The tidymodels workflow was:

Specify the model with linear_reg().
Fit it with fit(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento).
Get a tidy coefficient table with tidy(house_fit, conf.int = TRUE).

tidy() returns a data frame/tibble of model results, which can be plotted or saved.

Interpreting a continuous variable:

General sentence: > For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect [outcome] to increase or decrease by [estimate] [units], all else remaining the same.
For sqft: > For every 1 square foot increase in size, we expect the sale price to increase by $139, all else remaining the same.
“All else remaining the same” means the other predictors in the model, here type, are held fixed.
Units matter:

If a variable is standardized, one unit may mean one standard deviation.
If a variable is raw, one unit may be one square foot, one mg/dL, one kg/m², etc.


Interpreting a categorical variable:

General sentence: > We expect [outcome] for [level] to be [estimate] [units] higher or lower than for [reference level], all else remaining the same.
For typeMulti_Family: > We expect multi-family homes to sell for $66,224 less than condos, all else remaining the same.
For typeResidential: > We expect residential homes to sell for $8,253 more than condos, all else remaining the same.

Confidence interval includes 0:

For typeResidential, the 95% confidence interval went from about -$15,594 to $32,100.
Because the interval included 0, the data did not show a clear difference between residential homes and condos of the same size.
You still report the estimate and interval, but say the difference is unclear.

The intercept:

The intercept is the expected outcome when all continuous variables are 0 and all categorical variables are at their reference level.
In the house model, that would correspond to a condo with 0 square feet, which does not exist.
The instructor advised not to over-interpret the intercept in that setting.
It is still necessary for making predictions.

Prediction vs interpretation:

Interpretation asks: how does one predictor relate to the outcome while holding others fixed?
Prediction asks: given a specific house, what price does the model predict?
To predict, you use the intercept plus each predictor value multiplied by its coefficient.
Adding more predictors changes the coefficient values, but the interpretation skeleton for each individual coefficient remains the same.

Base R equivalent:

lm(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento) fits the same model.
Piping into tidy() gives the same coefficient table.
The instructor used tidymodels because the same workflow pattern can be used across many model types.






Data used in class:

licorice_gargle from the medicaldata package.
Trial of 235 adults having thoracic surgery with a large breathing tube.
Before the tube was inserted, patients were randomized to gargle licorice or sugar water.
Outcome: any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.

Recoding variables:

sore_throat:

Created from pacu30min_throatPain > 0.
Levels were no and yes.

treatment:

0 became sugar.
1 became licorice.

smoking:

3 became never.
2 became past.
1 became current.

bmi:

Selected from preOp_calcBMI.

drop_na() removed incomplete rows.

Which outcome level is modeled?

logistic_reg() models the odds of the outcome’s second factor level.
sore_throat had levels no then yes.
Therefore the model estimated the odds of yes, meaning having a sore throat.

Predictor structure:

treatment:

2 levels.
Produces 1 dummy variable.
Reference level: sugar.

bmi:

Continuous.
Units: kg/m².

smoking:

3 levels.
Produces 2 dummy variables.
Reference level: never.


Fitting the model:

The tidymodels workflow was:

Specify with logistic_reg().
Fit with fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking, data = sore).
Get coefficients with tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE).


Log-odds scale:

Logistic-regression coefficients are initially reported on the log-odds scale.
The log-odds transformation is:

log(p / (1 - p))

These values are hard to read directly.

Exponentiating coefficients:

Use tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) to convert estimates and confidence intervals to odds ratios.
std.error, statistic, and p.value remain on the log-odds scale.
An odds ratio of 1 means no difference.
Below 1 means lower odds.
Above 1 means higher odds.

Interpreting a continuous variable in logistic regression:

General sentence: > For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio], all else remaining the same.
For bmi: > For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI, we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by 0.95, all else remaining the same.
The interval included 1, so the data did not show a clear effect of BMI.

Interpreting categorical variables in logistic regression:

General sentence: > We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level] to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level], all else remaining the same.
For treatmentlicorice: > We expect the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice to be 0.384 times the odds for patients who gargled sugar water, all else remaining the same.
For smokingpast: > We expect the odds of a sore throat for past smokers to be 4.38 times the odds for people who never smoked, all else remaining the same.
smokingcurrent compares current smokers with people who never smoked, not with past smokers.

Odds are not probability:

An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities.
Say “0.38 times the odds,” not “0.38 times as likely” or “62% less likely.”
Odds and probability are close only when the outcome is rare.
In this dataset, about 27% of patients had a sore throat, so the distinction matters.

Reference levels:

The model can mathematically use any level as the reference.
The choice changes the sentences you write, even though the fitted model represents the same relationships.
If you care about a particular group, make that group the reference level by changing the factor levels.

Base R equivalent:

glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking, family = binomial, data = sore) fits the same logistic regression.
family = binomial is what makes glm() a logistic regression.
Piping into tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) gives the same odds ratios.






Agentic coding:

The instructor demonstrated using an AI coding agent, similar to GitHub Copilot in Codespaces or Claude, to help with the assignment.
The agent can read files, write code, run code, edit the .qmd file, and suggest changes.

Recommended workflow:

Ask it to answer one question or one small chunk at a time.
Do not ask it to do the entire assignment blindly.
Review the code it writes.
Run the code yourself and check the output.
If you do not understand a line, ask the agent to explain it.
You can guide it with class terminology, for example: “We learned pivot_longer() in class; can you use that?”

Privacy and safety:

Do not put passwords, API keys, or identifiable patient data into prompts or local files that an agent can read.
Coding agents may need to write code to print or inspect data.
If it prints patient data, that data may be sent to the model provider.
For hospital data, use only a hospital-sanctioned model or secure environment, not a personal subscription.
Agents can make mistakes, choose the wrong line to edit, or write code in a way you would not have written.
The human still has to review and understand the code.

Codespace agent safety:

An agent in a Codespace can access files in that environment.
It can read file contents, run code, and edit files.
The instructor emphasized that this is different from simply pasting text into a web chat.
The main protection is careful human review and not exposing sensitive files to the environment.

library(tidyverse)
This loaded the packages used for the tidy-data reshaping and dplyr work.



billboard_tidy <- read_csv("data/billboard.csv") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |>
  arrange(artist, track, week) |>
  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)
This recreated the analysis-oriented tidy Billboard table from Lecture 1. Each row represents one song’s rank for one week. pivot_longer() collapsed the weekly ranking columns, and mutate() calculated the chart date.
The result was a tibble with 5,307 rows and 7 columns:

Q: Was the Codespace we are using today “organic barnacle”? A: The Codespace names are randomly assigned. Each student may see a different name. Q: Do we have to fork the repository in order to do the work? A: No. Forking is optional for the session. It mainly gives you a copy in your own GitHub account. You can also work directly in the instructor’s Codespace or download the ZIP file if Git does not make sense yet.
Q: Does it matter what the reference value is? A: The model’s math still works no matter which level is chosen as the reference, but the interpretation sentence changes. It is usually better to choose a meaningful reference group, such as “never smoked” rather than an intermediate category. If you care about a particular group, you can change the factor levels so that group becomes the reference.
Q: Does it get more complicated to interpret if you have more covariates? A: No, not in the interpretation structure. You still interpret one coefficient at a time, holding all other variables in the model fixed. Adding more variables changes the numerical estimates, but the same sentence skeleton is used for each individual coefficient.
Q: If we add more variables after type, how do we look at price? A: There are two different tasks. If you are interpreting one variable, you isolate that coefficient and hold the others fixed. If you are predicting the price of a specific house, you use all the inputs: the intercept plus each predictor value multiplied by its coefficient, then add those pieces together.
Q: Is it possible to make a sentence about the reference value, such as the odds for someone who does not smoke? A: Usually the reference level is the baseline, and the other levels are interpreted relative to it. You generally do not interpret the reference level by itself in the same way. If you specifically want to compare everything to a particular group, make that group the reference level instead.
Q: If we end up doing the homework in R, how do we get the CSV? Is it part of a package? A: The dataset is provided in the course assignment folder or website. You can clone the repository or download the ZIP file. The main file to work from is the homework .qmd file.
Q: Are dates always printed as year, month, and day even though I wrote mdy()? A: Yes, that is expected if the input was a character string in month-day-year format. mdy() converts it into a Date object, and Date objects print in year-month-day order. If your input strings are already year-month-day, use ymd() instead.
Q: Is there an environment section in Codespaces where you can see variables like in RStudio? A: Codespaces is based on VS Code, which does not have the same variable viewer as RStudio. Positron does have a variable viewer. In Codespaces, you can print objects in a code chunk if you need to inspect them.
Q: Does closing the Codespace tab delete it? A: No. Closing the tab does not delete the Codespace. It may sleep or shut down after inactivity, but it can be restarted.
